articles.title: MicroQuanta, Zhejiang University achieve world-record efficiency of 23.9% for 19.48 cm² perovskite solar module
articles.description: The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.
paragraphs: A research team led by scientists from Chinese perovskite solar cell manufacturer MicroQuanta Semiconductor has achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% for a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module, setting a new world record.

The researchers said the result was enabled by cooling the wet perovskite precursor film before vacuum treatment to slow crystallization and reduce the fill factor losses associated with scaling up from cells to modules.

“What makes our result special is that the world record is achieved at the module level, rather than in a small laboratory cell,” corresponding author Dongchen Lan told pv magazine. “Solar cells often lose efficiency when scaled up into modules.”
The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.

Lan said the team identified a major cause of these losses and demonstrated a way to mitigate them while helping modules maintain their performance over time. “This addresses a key challenge in bringing next-generation solar technologies closer to practical use,” he said.

The researchers first compared laboratory-scale perovskite solar cells with mini-modules fabricated under matched processing conditions in previous studies. They used Shapley value analysis, which averages the contribution of each parameter across all possible orders of substitution, to quantify the contributions of open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, and fill factor to the measured efficiency loss.
After accounting for current losses in inactive areas created by laser scribing, they found that fill factor was the largest contributor to the efficiency drop from cells to modules.

To reduce that loss, the team spin-coated a perovskite precursor onto indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass carrying two hole-transport layers (HTLs). Immediately after coating, they cooled the wet film for 15 seconds to 0-10 C, transferred it to a vacuum chamber within about five seconds, and vacuum-flashed it for two minutes before annealing it at 110 C for 30 minutes. They then applied a surface passivation layer and deposited the electron-transport layers (ETLs) and silver (Ag) electrode. Measurements during film formation showed that cooling slowed the conversion of an intermediate phase into perovskite, yielding films with larger, more uniform grains.

The researchers used slot-die coating to fabricate a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module consisting of eight subcells connected in series through laser scribing. The device was built on a glass substrate coated with indium tin oxide (ITO), nickel oxide (NiOₓ), and a self-assembled monolayer known as 3PATAT-C3. It featured a formamidinium-cesium lead iodide (FA₀.₉₅Cs₀.₀₅PbI₃) absorber with an ethylenediammonium diiodide (EDAI₂) surface passivation layer, a fullerene (C₆₀) electron transport layer, a bathocuproine (BCP) buffer layer, and a silver (Ag) electrode.

According to the team’s measurements, the mini-module achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% and a fill factor of 83.3%, which the authors reported as the highest for a perovskite module. It also had a geometric fill factor of 97%, meaning 97% of its aperture area was photoactive. In separate aging tests under continuous one-sun illumination at open-circuit, the efficiency loss attributable to declining fill factor was less than one-third as large in modules made with the cooling step as in control modules.
articles.lede: The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.

articles.title: What’s behind the global solar slowdown
articles.description: BloombergNEF analyst Jenny Chase unpacks this year’s most surprising trends.
paragraphs: Since industry record-keeping began in 1976, global solar capacity has grown every single year. That streak, however, could end in 2026.

Every year since 2017, Jenny Chase, a solar and clean power analyst at BloombergNEF, has published an annual thread on social media outlining her most significant — and sometimes controversial — takes on the state of the global solar industry. In this year’s thread, she makes the case that this will be the global industry’s first down year for new builds.

In this episode, Shayle unpacks the highlights from Jenny’s solar “State of the Union.” They discuss her marquee prediction, and dig deeper to make sense of what this saturation point means for the global energy transition.

Some are popular, some decidedly are not, and all of them come from someone who’s been paying attention to this industry for two decades or so. At this point it’s kind of the closest thing solar has to a mini State of the Union. We actually did an episode going through some of her opinions once before back in 2022. I read the whole thread, I pick out the ones that I think are the most interesting or most surprising, and then unpack them with Jenny. The last time we did it was four years ago as I said, which in solar is a very long time, so seemed like time to do it again. Before we start, as I mentioned last week, we are going to wrap up 2026 with an Ask Me Anything episode. Send us your questions, you’ve got until December 8th to send them to [email protected]. We’ll answer as many as we can in the last episode of the year. In the meantime, Jenny Chase is coming up next. Jenny, welcome.

Solyco unveils 485 W full-black residential solar module with stainless steel protection
articles.description: The German manufacturer's new glass-glass solar panel features back-contact cells, a power conversion efficiency of 23.8% and a bifaciality factor of approximately 70%. It comes with a 30-year product warranty and an 88.85% power output guarantee after 30 years.
paragraphs: German solar module manufacturer Solyco has introduced a new full-black, glass-glass solar module for residential applications.

The Solyco Design R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect panel features a stainless steel cover for its connection cables, designed to protect them against mechanical damage, animal bites and ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

The module features 108 monocrystalline half-cut cells based on back-contact (BC) technology, delivering a power output of 485 W and a conversion efficiency of 23.8%. Under standard test conditions (STC), it has a maximum power voltage of 33.94 V and a maximum power current of 14.30 A. Its open-circuit voltage is 40.89 V, while its short-circuit current is 15.03 A.

The back-contact cell design places electrical connections on the rear of the cells, reducing front-side shading and providing a full-black appearance. The module has a bifaciality factor of around 70%. It features three separate junction boxes, each equipped with a bypass diode, with an IP68 protection rating. The 4 mm² solar cables are 1.2 m long and fitted with Stäubli MC4-Evo 2 connectors.
The module measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 24.8 kg. It features 2 mm tempered solar glass on both sides and a black-anodized aluminum frame.
The operating temperature ranges from -40 C to 85 C, with a nominal module operating temperature (NMOT) of 42 C. The temperature coefficient is -0.26%/C.

The module supports a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and a maximum reverse current of 30 A. It can withstand front-side loads of up to 5,400 Pa and rear-side loads of up to 2,400 Pa. The manufacturer also claims resistance to hailstones measuring up to 30 mm in diameter at impact speeds of 23.9 m/s.
Solyco offers a product warranty of up to 30 years and guarantees 88.85% of the module’s initial power output after 30 years.
According to the manufacturer, the R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect is its first commercially available module featuring integrated protection against animal bites for its connection cables.

Berlin-based Solyco Solar has expanded its portfolio of high-efficiency PV modules and specialized solar technologies in recent years. In July 2026, the company introduced a 500 W full-black back-contact module with an efficiency of 24.5%, following the launch of a 480 W back-contact panel in August 2025. The company has also developed a low-temperature solar cell interconnection technology designed to reduce material costs and vertical PV systems for green rooftops.
articles.lede: The German manufacturer's new glass-glass solar panel features back-contact cells, a power conversion efficiency of 23.8% and a bifaciality factor of approximately 70%.

Jackery and Every Electric launch 4 MWh plug-in battery VPP for New York renters
articles.description: Jackery has partnered with Brooklyn-based aggregator Every Electric to shift air conditioning load peaks without permitting limitations.
paragraphs: Portable power station manufacturer Jackery and consumer energy aggregator Every Electric have partnered to roll out what they call North America’s first plug-in battery aimed at renters and apartment residents.
By aggregating behind-the-meter storage, the setup uses standard wall outlets rather than hardwired residential systems that require electricians.

The tie-up is part of an Every Electric program that has operated across Consolidated Edison’s New York City service territory since September. Roughly 2,000 portable power stations, mostly Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, are currently distributed across more than 1,000 households, providing 4 MWh of flexible storage capacity. According to the companies, nearly 50 MWh of energy has cycled through the units to date.
The companies are calling it the “continent’s first plug-and-play virtual power plant (VPP) distribution network based on self-contained, expandable portable power stations”.

Onboarding requires residents to register online, link their utility account, and plug a window or portable air conditioner into the drop-shipped battery’s passthrough outlet. Once connected to Wi-Fi via Jackery’s app, Every Electric’s cloud software automates charging during off-peak hours and discharges the battery to run the air conditioner during peak grid demand, while keeping backup capacity available for outages.
The setup is similar to how plug-in storage has worked in Europe’s balcony solar market, and requires no electrician labor, municipal permits, or other agreements.
Every Electric offers options, both tied to a portable battery and an air conditioning unit.

A third option appears to be accepting a BYO battery as well, and Every Electric has details of operating with other brands outside of Jackery, with photos showing EcoFlow and Bluetti portable power stations.

“Traditional solar and storage require a roof, a garage or a permanent professional installation, which leaves renters and multifamily residents out,” said Andrew Wang, co-founder and CEO of Every Electric. “With Every Electric, adding grid services capabilities lets any household with a wall outlet earn on their bills while supporting the broader electrical infrastructure.”

Both companies are demonstrating the platform at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas from November 17 to 19, where Jackery is also exhibiting its modular Explorer 5000 Plus system with smart transfer switch support.

articles.title: Tesla seeks Texas tax break for $3.1 billion polysilicon plant
articles.description: Tesla says it will build a polysilicon plant in Texas only if the state cuts its property tax bill, as it seeks to produce solar’s most China-dominated material at home.
paragraphs: The application, filed with the Tuloso-Midway Independent School District under the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program, has been published by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts.

Tesla describes the plant as “under consideration for development” and as the “upstream component of Tesla’s vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform.” It says that “in the absence of the agreement the applicant would not make the proposed investment in this state” and that it is assessing locations in other jurisdictions.

The plant would produce ultra-high-purity polysilicon for single-crystal silicon ingots and N-type, high-efficiency solar cells. Its equipment list includes a hydrochlorination and trichlorosilane synthesis unit, chlorosilane distillation and purification trains, silicon tetrachloride recycling loops and Siemens chemical vapor deposition reactors. The filing does not state the plant’s production capacity.
Tesla said in the filing that more than 90% of the world’s solar-grade polysilicon is produced in China.

Under the schedule in the EY analysis, the project’s taxable value for school-district maintenance and operations taxes would be cut to zero from 2028 to 2030 and halved from 2031 through 2040. The Comptroller must review the application, and both the Office of the Governor and the school district’s board must approve an agreement before it takes effect.

The US government’s Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon, which also impose a 15% duty on imported ingots, wafers, cells and modules, take effect on Dec. 4. The minimum import prices are designed to force foreign suppliers to match US production costs, raising the value of domestic feedstock in a market where US polysilicon production remains limited. Solar manufacturer Toyo secured US polysilicon supply to navigate trade barriers in January.

Tesla has been advancing a plan to build 100 GW of US PV manufacturing capacity by 2028, a target that has drawn scrutiny over whether Elon Musk’s solar ambitions are achievable. The company has taken a similar approach in storage, where it said in 2025 that its 10 GWh lithium iron phosphate cell factory in Nevada was nearing completion as it reduced reliance on imported cells.

At COP31, Longi details its pathways to advance global green development
articles.description: Floria Wang, Head of Global Branding at LONGi, delivered a keynote speech at a side event on implementation and highlighted the company’s practical achievements in advancing the global energy transition.
paragraphs: The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) ran from 9 to 20 November 2026. On 11 November, at the side event “Clean Energy Systems: From NDCs to Implementation” – hosted by the Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization (GEIDCO) at the UNFCCC Capacity Building Hub – Floria Wang, Head of Global Branding at LONGi, delivered a keynote speech in which she shared the company’s practical achievements in advancing the global energy transition.

For diverse industrial fields such as manufacturing, construction, and logistics, LONGi provides customized photovoltaic and energy storage solutions that help enterprises replace traditional fossil fuels with clean electricity, effectively reducing operating costs and carbon footprints while enabling low-carbon and intelligent industrial transformation and upgrading.

LONGi actively promotes the “energy + rural revitalization” development model in many developing regions. For example, since 2024, Shaanxi Province has been rolling out the “PV+” rural revitalization demonstration project, under which the government provides overall coordination; village collectives establish village-owned new energy companies as the investment and loan entities; and farming households only provide rooftop space and bear no investment or loan risk. LONGi is responsible for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the power stations, while State Grid Shaanxi is responsible for grid capacity expansion and upgrading. Banks provide long-term green inclusive loans with an 18-year term. Power generation revenue is first used to repay loan principal and interest; after deducting loan repayments and operation and maintenance costs, net revenue is distributed between the village company and villagers at a ratio of 2:8. In addition, the project offers the option of installing air-source heat pumps, with dividend income from power generation covering heating expenses, allowing villagers to enjoy clean winter heating free of charge.

By integrating photovoltaic technology into urban buildings, public infrastructure, and transportation systems, LONGi helps cities build distributed clean energy networks, providing an energy foundation for smart city operations and bringing the benefits of green, low-carbon living to the wider public.

For remote regions with inadequate grid infrastructure, LONGi deploys off-grid and microgrid solar-storage systems, using clean energy to light up remote villages, ensure electricity for local healthcare, education, and people’s basic daily needs, and help address energy accessibility challenges in certain areas.

articles.description: Bolivia’s state-owned utility ENDE is seeking an EPC contractor for a project scheduled for completion in June 2028. The solar plant will be financed in part by a loan from German development bank KfW.
paragraphs: Bolivia’s state-owned power utility ENDE has launched an international tender for the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) of the Contorno Bajo I solar plant, which will have a minimum nominal capacity of 40 MWac. The project will become the first large-scale solar power plant in the department of La Paz.

The tender, published on Nov. 16 under reference ENDE-KFW-2026-002, sets a 14-month implementation period from the signing of the contract. Construction is scheduled to begin in May 2027, with commissioning expected to be completed by June 2028.

The contract includes a 24.9/115 kV step-up substation, an approximately 800-meter-long, 115 kV interconnection line, and modifications to a bay at the Contorno Bajo substation, owned by ENDE Transmisión, to feed electricity into Bolivia’s National Interconnected System (SIN).

A separate tender for consulting and project supervision services is also underway, with bids due by Dec. 21. The contract covers construction supervision, equipment quality control, plant commissioning and training for ENDE personnel.

According to information released by ENDE in July, the solar plant will occupy 34 hectares at an altitude of more than 3,700 meters above sea level and will have an estimated operational lifetime of 25 years.
The original project design, announced in January 2023, included a lithium-ion battery energy storage system. However, the current tender notice makes no mention of a storage component.

articles.description: À Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, la Société du Canal de Provence (SCP) et la Région Sud ont développé un démonstrateur de couverture photovoltaïque de 71 mètres. Son objectif est de conjuguer production d’électricité renouvelable et transport de l’eau, sans artificialiser de nouvelles surfaces.
paragraphs: The Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur regional government and Société du Canal de Provence (SCP) have completed what they describe as France’s first large-scale canal-top PV project in Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, in the Var department.

Spanning 71 meters, the custom-designed installation covers the canal and its banks, demonstrating a new approach that combines water transport and electricity generation on the same infrastructure. With an installed capacity of 299 kW and estimated annual generation of 404 MWh, the pilot project accounts for approximately 1% of SCP’s annual energy consumption.
SCP has a long history in hydropower and currently operates 17 small hydroelectric plants, generating approximately 17 GWh per year. The company plans to expand this capacity in the coming years.

SCP aims to become a net energy producer, eventually generating more renewable electricity than its estimated annual consumption of 40 GWh. Since the early 2020s, the company has been adding solar PV to its existing hydropower portfolio.

Developed under the regional concession for the Canal de Provence, the pilot project also aims to help control water service costs. It makes use of existing infrastructure without requiring additional land development, while potentially improving water quality through the shading provided by the solar panels.

With nearly 70 km of open-air canals, the Canal de Provence, part of the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region’s hydraulic infrastructure, offers significant potential for solar PV development. SCP studies estimate that the canals could accommodate more than 50 MW of PV capacity, generating approximately 70 GWh of electricity annually.
However, deployment will be selective, with only 5% to 10% of the canal network considered suitable for PV installations due to technical and regulatory constraints.

In October, French manufacturer Holosolis secured support under the EU Innovation Fund for its planned 5 GW solar cell and module factory in Hambach, France. The project was among 77 net-zero technology initiatives selected for a combined €3.4 billion in funding, including investments in solar, battery and other clean-energy manufacturing technologies.

Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar by 2029 with policy reforms
articles.description: IESR says Indonesia could achieve most of its 100 GW of solar by 2029 target through coordinated utility-scale procurement, rooftop PV deployment, diesel replacement and rural electrification, but warns regulatory and grid barriers need to be addressed.
paragraphs: Indonesia’s cumulative installed solar capacity reached 1.59 GW as of the first quarter of 2026 (Q1 2026), according to the latest report from the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), a Jakarta-based think tank.
IESR’s Indonesia Solar Energy Outlook 2027 says the figure is equivalent to around 1.5% of Indonesia’s power generation capacity and 0.3% of electricity production.

Rooftop PV currently accounts for the largest share of installed capacity, standing at 0.9 GW as of Q1 2026. Utility-scale solar accounted for 0.33 GW, captive solar for 0.3 GW and installations in remote areas for around 0.06 GW.

With the country passing the 1 GW solar milestone in 2025, IESR says the current growth rate is “far behind the government’s ambition to make solar power one of the backbones of the national energy system”, as set out in the country’s 100 GW solar power program which President Prabowo Subianto has set a target of achieving by 2029.
The program officially launched in August with a first phase of 14 projects totalling around 5.2 GW, but only 526 MW of this capacity currently have targeted completion dates, IESR’s report reveals.
The think tank adds that deployments are currently held back by regulatory gaps, procurement uncertainty and limited grid access.

In a statement sent to pv magazine, IESR CEO Fabby Tumiwa said the 100 GW ambition needs to be reflected in updates to Indonesia’s 2025-2034 electricity supply business plan (RUPTL), with greater emphasis on utility-scale PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS), diesel replacement with solar-plus-storage and rooftop PV deployment.
IESR’s modelling suggests Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar capacity by 2029 if development proceeds through multiple channels simultaneously.

The report says around 8 GW is already planned through RUPTL and Mentari GigaOne procurements, while a further 56 GW could come through procurements by Indonesia’s state-owned electric utility PLN. It suggests the remaining 33 GW could be developed through rooftop PV, diesel replacement, rural electrification, captive solar and other distributed applications.
IESR says five enablers that must move together – demand, rooftop access, procurement, grid and supply chain – will determine whether the 100 GW scales.

Efficient heating is not enough: Why the timing of electricity use matters for heat pumps
articles.description: Operating a heat pump as cost-effectively as possible involves more than just monitoring electricity prices. In many cases, shifting electricity consumption to different times is neither feasible nor practical. Matthias Martensen, CEO and co-founder of Ostrom, explains the factors that determine how flexibly heat pumps can use electricity.
paragraphs: When discussing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps, the focus is usually on the seasonal performance factor (SPF), flow temperature and building insulation. While these factors remain crucial, the debate around dynamic electricity tariffs is too narrow if it focuses solely on how long a heat pump can be switched off. What matters is the overall flexibility of a household’s electricity consumption.

On very cold winter days, well-designed heat pumps often need to run almost continuously, leaving little scope for shifting heat production. At milder temperatures, however, there is some flexibility: Buildings and hot water storage tanks can retain heat for several hours. For example, a home can be preheated overnight for the morning or during the day for the evening. Similarly, hot water production can be scheduled for periods when electricity prices are lower. How long this flexibility lasts depends on the building’s insulation, heating system and storage capacity, although it is generally insufficient to bridge entire days.

Even when a heat pump runs continuously, the electricity it consumes does not necessarily have to be drawn from the grid at the same time. A suitable battery storage system can charge from the grid when electricity prices are low and supply power later. In this case, it is not heat production that is shifted, but the timing of electricity drawn from the grid. This distinction is particularly relevant for households with photovoltaic systems and existing battery storage.

In summer, PV systems cover a larger share of household electricity demand with self-generated solar power. In winter, heating demand increases while solar power generation declines, making households more dependent on grid electricity. An existing battery storage system, provided it supports grid charging and can be controlled in response to electricity prices, can therefore do more than store solar power. It can also take advantage of periods of low wholesale electricity prices.

For households that already have battery storage, the economics are different. The key question is whether the potential savings from price differences outweigh additional storage losses, battery degradation and any costs associated with technical modifications. Even then, profitable operation is far from guaranteed. Average hourly prices also do not reflect the price differences that can actually be exploited on individual days. While the figures illustrate the importance of when electricity is drawn from the grid, they do not demonstrate actual savings.

Other flexible loads also play a role. Households charging electric vehicles, particularly in winter, often cannot rely solely on electricity generated by their own PV systems. Coordinated energy management can help shift charging to periods when grid electricity is cheaper. Even when solar generation is low, strong wind power output can drive down wholesale electricity prices.

For heat pumps, electricity prices are not the only factor affecting operating costs. With air-to-water heat pumps, outdoor temperatures also matter. If temperatures are higher around midday than in the early morning, the system can operate more efficiently. An intelligent control system should therefore consider electricity prices, outdoor temperatures and actual heating demand simultaneously. Producing additional heat simply because electricity is cheap makes little sense if that heat is ultimately wasted.
articles.lede: Operating a heat pump as cost-effectively as possible involves more than just monitoring electricity prices. In many cases, shifting electricity consumption to different times is neither feasible nor practical.

articles.title: Wisconsin’s new Dem trifecta could be a boon for clean energy
articles.description: The state lags behind its neighbors in transitioning to renewables. Now policymakers have the chance to overcome logjams on community solar and more.
paragraphs: The Democratic sweep in this year’s midterm elections has opened up new opportunities for advancing the clean energy transition in states across the country. That’s particularly true in Wisconsin, where Democrats will have a trifecta for the first time in 16 years, and which has lagged behind its Midwestern neighbors on renewables.

Indeed, Gov.-elect David Crowley (D) and legislative leaders have pledged to promote clean energy as a way to address affordability and meet demand from planned data centers. Advocates say they have already been talking with legislators and drafting proposals that they hope will advance once new lawmakers take office on Jan. 4.

“ It’s very exciting to see these changes,” said Beata Wierzba, government affairs director at RENEW Wisconsin, a nonprofit advocacy group that works to advance clean energy policies. ​ “ The Democratic leadership has a very ambitious agenda, which includes clean energy and renewables. We know we’re on their plate.”

Last spring, Democratic state lawmakers introduced a bill mandating that Wisconsin electricity generation be 100 % emissions-free by 2050. The bill did not advance, but clean energy advocates are hoping a similar initiative will be a top priority for the new Democratic legislature. The only such mandate on the books right now is woefully outdated, calling for 10 % renewable energy by 2015. The state has long surpassed that, with a fifth of the electricity delivered to customers currently coming from renewables.

Shifting to net-zero emissions by 2050 — including 100 % clean energy — would create over 68, 000 jobs and avoid at least $ 2 billion in healthcare costs, according to a report by RENEW, the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, and other groups.

Abby Novinska-Lois, executive director of the nonprofit public health advocacy group Healthy Climate Wisconsin, noted that ​ “ Wisconsin is really behind” states like Illinois — which mandates fossil-fuel-free electricity generation by 2045 — when it comes to emissions that harm the climate and public health.

“ We think all Wisconsinites deserve the freedom to have cleaner air and cleaner water and the [lower] bills that come with clean energy,” she said. ​ “ We are hearing interest from policymakers that they want to accelerate affordable energy for all Wisconsinites. We know clean energy is the most affordable.”

Right now in Wisconsin, only utilities can build solar arrays that provide energy to customers. Twenty-four states plus Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, allow companies other than utilities to build community solar, including Wisconsin’s neighbor Illinois, which provides robust incentives.
“ Now with the Democratic majority, we might be able to work something out where both sides will see it’s good for the workers and good for the people,” Wierzba said.

For almost a decade, Wisconsin has been a battleground over third-party-owned distributed solar. Under such arrangements, a solar developer owns the array that provides power to a home, business, organization, or government agency. The model eliminates up-front costs for the customer and helps nonprofits and government entities tap tax incentives that might not otherwise be available since they don’t pay taxes. But the state’s largest utility, We Energies, has long argued that this lets solar developers illegally act as utilities. Solar advocates and developers want a law to clarify that third-party-owned solar is legal so that projects can move forward.
articles.lede: The state lags behind its neighbors in transitioning to renewables. Now policymakers have the chance to overcome logjams on community solar and more.

articles.title: Massachusetts pilot program offers free batteries and extra cash
articles.description: In Fall River, low-income families can receive a free home battery and a yearly stipend as part of a utility program to reduce grid strain and electricity…
paragraphs: A Massachusetts utility has announced plans to use home batteries to help 125 low-income families save money and keep the lights on during power outages — all at no cost to them. If successful, the pilot program could serve as a model for similar initiatives throughout the state, as utilities pursue a mandate to create a more affordable, robust, and equitable electric system.

National Grid this month launched BatteryBackup+, a partnership with residential power-storage company Haven Energy that will bring the no-cost batteries to homes in Fall River, a working-class former mill city where the median household income hovers just above half the statewide average.

Participants will receive a battery capable of providing at least four hours of backup power, as well as $ 150 annually for five years. To qualify, residents must already be signed up for National Grid’s low-income discount rate, or meet the equivalent income limits — about $ 103, 000 per year for a four-person household, for example.

Haven will handle installation and maintenance of the systems, and manage the batteries’ enrollment and deployment in programs that share their power with the grid to alleviate strain at times of high demand. After 10 years, participants will be able to work with Haven to take over ownership and management of the batteries or remove them. The utility’s overall goal is to develop and refine a strategy for making the grid more efficient and resilient while giving a financial boost to families who are the most vulnerable to soaring energy prices.
“ We’re really excited about what we get to learn from this,” said Joshua Tom, National Grid’s director of energy transition solutions.

The idea of aggregating residential batteries to create benefits for the grid is not new. When batteries work in concert to send power into the system, it can reduce the need for energy from pricier, dirtier plants. In the long term, such arrangements can also help avoid expensive grid upgrades that would be paid for by customers.

States are increasingly leaning into the concept. Vermont’s Green Mount Power harnesses this potential with a network of 10, 000 residential batteries. Massachusetts’ ConnectedSolutions model, launched as a pilot in 2016, has been adopted or adapted by nearby states including Connecticut and Rhode Island. New Jersey just launched its own program paying residents to share their battery capacity with the grid.

Haven’s business model takes advantage of this trend. As in the Fall River pilot, the company handles the installation and management of residential batteries. Haven then earns money from enrolling the equipment in state programs, using some of the revenue to make the investment more affordable for customers.

Haven currently operates in seven states — including elsewhere in Massachusetts — with eight more coming soon. In most places, customers pay a monthly fee for their batteries and the company’s services, starting at $ 29.

Fall River is not Haven’s first foray into a no-cost model. Last year, the company launched a program in California providing free batteries to low-income households. So far, the program has contracted with about 2, 500 homes and completed installations in about 60 % of them.
articles.lede: A Massachusetts utility has announced plans to use home batteries to help 125 low-income families save money and keep the lights on during power outages — all at no cost to them.

articles.title: How solar and storage are powering a new era of American manufacturing
articles.description: The Steel River Energy Center in Arkansas will help supply electricity to U. S. Steel’s Big River Steel mill, offering a model for how utility-scale…
paragraphs: In the early 2020 s, U. S. Steel launched a nationwide search to find the best location for a new factory. The company had recently completed its acquisition of the Big River Steel mill in Osceola, Arkansas. The goal of the expansion: Replicate the success of Big River Steel, which supplies the automotive, construction, and renewable-energy industries and can produce over 3 million tons of steel annually.

After an exhaustive search, the company realized there was no reason to look beyond Northeast Arkansas. ​ “ We went to 48 states and narrowed the site selection down to 20, 10, five, and then three,” said Dan Brown, U. S. Steel’s executive vice president of advanced technology steelmaking and CEO of Big River Steel. ​ “ We built another plant one mile from where we’re at.” At close to $ 3. 5 billion, the investment in what is now called Big River Steel 2 was the largest in U. S. Steel’s storied 125 -year history.

A variety of factors go into determining the ideal location of a steel plant, including proximity to large customers, good railroad and river transportation, and a solid local workforce. Arguably most important, however, is access to reliable and affordable electricity, because producing steel requires an enormous amount of power. ​ “ If that isn’t number one, it’s in the top two,” Brown said. ​ “ You have to have a good electricity provider and a good electricity source.”

The reliable, affordable energy source that will help power the growth of one of America’s most iconic manufacturers is solar and energy storage. To that end, the Steel River Energy Center, which broke ground this past July, is a 2. 46 -gigawatt solar and 2. 94 -gigawatt-hour battery storage facility that will be built in three phases and is expected to be fully operational in 2029. Cypress Creek Energy is developing, and will own and operate, what will be the largest solar project with energy storage in America.

The Steel River Energy Center is notable for a host of reasons. The grid-connected project represents $ 4. 5 billion in private investment and is expected to create 1, 400 construction jobs in its first two phases and generate $ 300 million in local tax revenue over its lifetime. Google also signed a power purchase agreement ( PPA) with Cypress Creek Energy to secure the energy produced by the first two phases of the project. The Steel River Energy Center is the largest solar and storage project Google has sourced energy from worldwide.

Whether it’s the project’s size, offtake agreement, job creation, or tax revenue, much about the Steel River Energy Center attracts superlatives. But less obvious, and more meaningful for U.S. communities far beyond Mississippi County, Arkansas is the example it provides of solar and storage’s ability to power even the most energy-intensive industries and the many benefits of a robust domestic supply chain.

“ Ten years ago, solar was still pretty niche, and battery storage was hardly on the radar,” said Kevin Smith, CEO of Cypress Creek Energy. ​ “ Steel River is proof that solar and storage have crossed a threshold. This is not niche energy dependent on incentives. This is the foundation of American industrial competitiveness, because we can beat alternatives on price and speed, both of which are critical to businesses that depend on affordable and reliable energy.”
articles.lede: Steel launched a nationwide search to find the best location for a new factory. The company had recently completed its acquisition of the Big River Steel mill in Osceola, Arkansas.

articles.title: Remote control and cybersecurity: Protecting renewable energy plants’ digital infrastructure
articles.description: SCADA systems, inverters, plant controllers and remote access points are becoming critical cybersecurity vulnerabilities at renewable energy plants, while the EU’s NIS2 Directive and evolving cybersecurity requirements are driving stricter standards for system protection, authentication, access management and incident response.
paragraphs: Modern solar and wind farms are highly interconnected industrial facilities. Their operation depends on SCADA systems, plant controllers, weather stations, grid protection equipment, communication gateways and, in some cases, cloud platforms provided by equipment manufacturers or plant operators.

Remote control capabilities are essential to the operation of Spain’s electricity system. Red Eléctrica’s Renewable Energy Control Center (CECRE) monitors more than 4,500 renewable energy generation facilities in real time. Facilities, or groups of facilities, with an installed capacity exceeding 1 MW are monitored through telemetry data. The system operator can also transmit setpoints to regulate their output and maintain the balance between electricity generation and demand.
Do you want to strengthen and enhance the cybersecurity of your solar energy assets to safeguard them against emerging threats?
Join us on Dec. 3 for pv magazine Week Europe 2026 | Cyber winter: Is Europe’s solar sector ready for the stress test?

Industry experts will explore real-world cyberattack scenarios, highlight potential vulnerabilities in solar and storage systems, and share practical, actionable strategies to protect your energy assets. Attendees will gain valuable knowledge on how to anticipate, prevent, and respond to cyber threats in the rapidly evolving solar energy sector.

The regulatory framework is primarily based on Royal Decree 413/2014, electricity system operating procedures and European grid connection requirements. Operating Procedure P.O. 9.2 governs the exchange of real-time information with the system operator and establishes communication requirements between generation facilities, control centers and the system operator.

Following amendments introduced by a resolution dated June 19, 2026, failure to comply with real-time data transmission requirements may also result in financial penalties. On cybersecurity, Article 4, Section 9.2, explicitly states:

“Both the SO’s control centers and the control centers authorized to exchange real-time information with the SO shall be responsible for ensuring protection against cyberattacks originating from their respective control centers.”

Remote control is associated with electricity system operations. The system operator can transmit setpoints or other operational instructions to a generation facility through an authorized control center. Red Eléctrica publishes a list of authorized control centers that have passed setpoint-following tests and are qualified to manage the integration of renewable energy generation facilities into the grid.

Remote access, by contrast, is used for operation and maintenance activities. Inverter manufacturers, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors, operation and maintenance (O&M) providers and plant operators may remotely connect to inverters, plant controllers or SCADA systems to monitor equipment, diagnose faults, update software, adjust configurations or provide technical support.

articles.title: Outage fears rise, but batteries — and gas
articles.description: NERC found that just three areas are at “elevated” blackout risk this winter.
paragraphs: The North American power grid is less at risk of blackouts this winter than it was this time last year, according to a reliability watchdog.

The North American Electric Reliability Corp. found that just three areas are at “elevated” risk during cold snaps — meaning there wouldn’t be enough reserved capacity to meet peak demand — down from seven a year ago.

NERC attributed the improvement to the addition of more than 26 gigawatts of winter peak capacity, driven by about nine gigawatts of both battery storage and gas generation. California and Texas led the pack in terms of deploying storage, while Texas, northern Mexico, and the Mountain West accounted for the largest gas expansions.

The Department of Energy’s emergency orders allowing grid operators to order data centers and other large facilities to shift to backup generators during peak demand — even if it involves breaching air pollution limits — is also helping shore up the grid, NERC found. So are DOE orders keeping six fossil fuel plants online past their scheduled retirement dates, even as they raise costs for customers and greenhouse gas emissions.

In the U.S., just North and South Carolina remain in the “elevated” risk category amid rapid growth in residential electric heating and the arrival of large data centers and industrial loads. That growth has steadily eroded reserve margins, NERC said, particularly during early morning hours before solar generation ramps up. Canadian provinces including Quebec and Nova Scotia are also at elevated risk, mainly because gas pipelines are constrained.

NERC’s assessment comes as Americans grow increasingly concerned about the reliability of the U.S. power grid. Outages are getting longer, mainly due to more extreme weather as global temperatures rise from burning fossil fuels. Utilities and grid operators are struggling to modernize and expand their systems fast enough to keep up with demand from data centers, reshored manufacturing, and a more electrified economy.

And in recent days, fears of nationwide blackout spread across TikTok and other social media platforms due to a false, manipulated clip of President Donald Trump from an account pushing cryptocurrency, Politifact reported. Further fueling the anxiety have been a series of technology failures impacting air travel, banks, Microsoft, and Apple.

Beyond reliability, NERC also oversees cybersecurity threats to the bulk power system, including by enforcing mandatory standards for utilities and grid operators aimed at preventing cyber and physical attacks on electric, natural gas, and transmission infrastructure. NERC is also the primary hub for companies to share sensitive cyber incident data, indicators of attacks, and vulnerability alerts.

In January, NERC said that these mandatory security controls remain critical, but they aren’t being updated fast enough to keep up with changing threats. That report said a major vulnerability can be addressed by requiring employees or third-party vendors connecting remotely to smaller energy sites to use two-step login verifications. That includes solar, wind, and battery projects, as well as substations and fossil fuel plants. This is already required of the largest power plants, transmission hubs, and regional control centers.
articles.lede: NERC found that just three areas are at “elevated” blackout risk this winter.

articles.title: Utilities want FERC to lock data centers into paying for grid upgrades
articles.description: Their FERC filings would require data centers to cover costs for 10 to 20 years, longer than some states require.
paragraphs: A year ago, Energy Secretary Chris Wright directed federal regulators to speed up how data centers and other large power users get connected to the grid. Then in June, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s initial view was that the existing rules fell short; it ordered the six grid operators it oversees to show how they would fix them.
By Nov. 16, five had answered. The sixth, the Southwest Power Pool, is due to file by Nov. 20.

The operators’ plans are, unsurprisingly, mostly about speed. The plans focus on shorter timelines and earlier connections for data centers. PJM would study new load and new generation together in a single 12-month process, for example. New York and California took similar approaches, both proposing to let data centers connect faster to the grid if they agree to curtail during periods of congestion.

But the operators weren’t the only ones to file this week. The utilities that own the transmission lines also sent in their own proposals, grouped by region. Their responses tackle a different question: not how to get loads connected faster, but rather who pays for the associated grid upgrades and for how long?

And while each takes a different approach to answering that question, together they are asking FERC to endorse an approach where data centers sign a long-term contract with the utility that owns the relevant lines before the upgrades it needs can get built.

For the utilities in PJM’s region, a data center would commit to paying for at least 80% of the transmission service it requests for a minimum of 10 years, backed by collateral. In California and New York, the term would be 15 years. The Midwest is proposing a more unusual set-up, as its main grid operator, MISO, pitched the contract itself: a three-way agreement with the utility and the data center that would run up to 20 years.

If those commitments look familiar, it’s because they are. Many of the same utilities already require similar terms for data center customers under tariffs their state regulators approved. Now, though, they’re using the show-cause order as an opportunity to ask FERC to approve something similar — though crucially, not exactly the same. The federal proposals ask data centers for longer commitments in some places, and shorter ones in others.

A data center’s power bill is regulated in two places. The state utility commission approves the utility’s tariff, which sets what the customer pays for local lines, power plants, and, in some states, transmission. Then FERC regulates the high-voltage grid, which is where the new contracts would sit.
These new contracts cover only transmission and don’t replace the state tariff, so a data center could end up signing two parallel, but not identical, sets of terms.

For utilities in PJM, the federal half would be a cost recovery agreement that the data center signs directly with the transmission owner, requiring the data center to pay at least 80% of its expected transmission charges. The data center would also have to put up a financial guarantee starting at 25% of what it would owe, and increasing to the full amount by the time service begins. A data center that leaves early would owe the transmission owner the rest.
articles.lede: Their FERC filings would require data centers to cover costs for 10 to 20 years, longer than some states require.

articles.title: Anthropic debuts in an uneasy energy week
articles.description: The AI lab is going public just a day after a much-watched Nvidia earnings call.
paragraphs: Nvidia ousted CEO Jensen Huang over his multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese spy; the blue wave midterm election involved a significant data center backlash; there are signs of a slowdown in data center construction. And all come just as investors have grown concerned about AI’s promise and enormous expenditures.

But if the AI bubble appeared to be losing some air, Anthropic’s market debut and a strong showing in Nvidia’s earnings yesterday might pump things up again, according to Morningstar senior equity analyst Travis Miller. And that’s good news for the many energy companies that have served the boom; Miller monitors electric utilities, which he said have had a “rough” couple of weeks.

“Utilities and investors are watching the landscape very closely because data center growth is a key part of the investment story for utilities in the coming years,” Miller said. “Can utilities continue to live up to investor expectations of growth if the bubble is deflating?”

Anthropic’s updated financial report to the Securities and Exchange Commission walks through the infrastructure buildout that the company sees ahead (a lot) and how the company is thinking about energy (also a lot).

As an AI lab, of course, Anthropic doesn’t develop data centers itself. But it contracts a huge, and swiftly growing, number of them. They rely heavily on fossil fuels, according to a recent analysis, and Anthropic’s prospectus includes little encouragement for clean energy suppliers. The company makes just one brief mention of clean energy sources such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, warning that those “may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost.”
Discover what bring-your-own-capacity offers C&I projects and how new market structures can make distributed batteries bankable
Energy concerns are clearly front of mind. The company dedicated much of its assessment of risks to a discussion of the variability and uncertainties of power supplies and regulations.
“Electric grid infrastructure in the United States and other countries was not designed to accommodate the rapid increase in demand associated with AI development,” the AI lab wrote.

An analysis of Anthropic’s energy use by the nonprofit Better Data Center Project reveals just how fossil-bound the company is. The researcher’s case study found that Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S.

The company’s data centers are mostly sited in areas where the grid relies heavily on coal and gas, and “currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term.” Lacking commitments to clean energy, the additional demand on the grid post-IPO will likely mean more fossil infrastructure. When the company uses behind-the-meter sources, the researchers said, the gas-burning turbines are often less efficient and more polluting.
articles.lede: The AI lab is going public just a day after a much-watched Nvidia earnings call.

“Repowering” worn out solar fields could create gigawatts of new grid capacity, quickly
articles.description: A conversation with Lisa Hansmann of Foundry-Logic.
paragraphs: America’s first big wave of solar power installations, built between 15 and 20 years ago, is hitting middle age. With failing inverters and expiring contracts, they are underperforming just as the grid needs more capacity. Lisa Hansmann of Foundry-Logic argues that some of the fastest, cheapest new capacity is hiding in solar and battery plants we’ve already built. Rebuild them with better panels and batteries and existing grid connections can deliver much more.

The first big wave of American solar farms went up between 2010 and 2016. Those installations, now 15+ years old, are getting creaky. Their inverters are failing, their panels’ output is declining, and their power contracts are running out.

The thing is, with interconnection queues so clogged and slow, the most valuable parts of an old solar array are often its land and its connection to the grid, not its panels. If you replace old panels with new, more efficient ones, and add batteries, you can squeeze a lot more useful power through existing, underutilized grid connections — relatively quickly, in months rather than years.

That's the idea behind repowering, as described in a new report from Crux, a clean energy finance firm, and Foundry-Logic, a company that Biden advisor and previous Volts guest Brian Deese co-founded to operate, maintain, and upgrade energy equipment that's already installed. The report estimates repowering could unlock the equivalent of up to 67 gigawatts of solar and 92 gigawatts of batteries by 2040. Those are ceilings, though, and the question is how close we can get to them in practice.

To talk through it with us, I’ve got one of the report’s authors, Lisa Hansmann, a director at Foundry-Logic. She worked in the Biden White House implementing the IRA and infrastructure laws; she and Deese have argued that the quickest new capacity is hiding in the existing grid. We’re going to get into what repowering costs, how much it involves inverters and batteries rather than panels, and what kinds of solar sites Foundry plans to go after first. Let’s jump in.
Crux and Foundry-Logic - Recharged: Repowering America’s Solar Fleet with Storage for a New Era of Demand
David Roberts: All right, let’s jump in. With no further ado, Lisa Hansmann, welcome to Volts. Thank you so much for coming.

David Roberts: Excited to talk about this. But before we get into the specifics, before we get into the repowering stuff, I want to talk a little bit about the Foreign Affairs piece that you and Brian Deese wrote. So you and Brian both worked in the White House, and then you worked with him at MIT for a while on his research team. What did you see and learn together that led you to this central argument you make in the Foreign Affairs piece? So maybe just tell us the central argument, and then tell us what brought you to it.

Lisa Hansmann: Yeah. So the central argument is that against the backdrop of a truly historic supply-demand imbalance in electricity markets, the fastest source of capacity is from optimizing the grid and the assets that we already have. And to take you through the long and winding path of how we got here, I got thrown into energy policy when I worked on the Biden administration after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. I joined the administration as a generalist economic policy advisor at the National Economic Council, where I worked with Brian. And after Russia invaded Ukraine, all of a sudden it seemed like we were facing what now in retrospect seems to be a relatively quaint disruption in conventional energy.
articles.lede: A conversation with Lisa Hansmann of Foundry-Logic.

articles.title: Why utilities should design VPPs around households, not devices
articles.description: Single-device programs treat household change as churn. A portfolio built around households turns it into durable grid capacity.
paragraphs: This is partner content, brought to you by ev.energy. Nate Kinsey is the company’s director of policy.

Residential virtual power plants aren’t a new pitch. Utilities and regulators have heard for more than a decade that thermostats, home batteries, heat pumps, and EVs could be coordinated by the thousands to act like a power plant. What’s new is the urgency. Load is growing for the first time in two decades; bills are rising; and the poles, wires, and power plants needed to keep up take years to build.

This year, states started acting. Hawaii opened a VPP docket in April, Virginia approved a ratepayer-funded VPP pilot in August, and last week New Jersey regulators approved a two-year statewide VPP program, PowerUp NJ, set to launch by October 1, 2027. Virginia’s and New Jersey’s programs start where VPPs always have: cutting system peak demand. That’s the right first step, but it isn’t where the opportunity ends.

Distribution spending is now among the fastest-growing parts of utility budgets, and New Jersey’s own program envisions VPPs moving from peak-shaving to deferring or avoiding traditional infrastructure upgrades. Getting there means moving VPPs down the grid, from the system peak to the feeder and substation, and moving dispatch events from the peak to everyday grid operations.

That’s where utilities remain skeptical. At Latitude Media’s Flex Summit in October, Eversource’s director of distributed energy solutions put it plainly: “What happens if they’re not there in 10 years?” A substation takes a decade to build. There is no plan B.
The skepticism is fair. The honest answer is that the same devices won’t be there. The question for regulators is whether the capacity will be, and that depends on how we design the programs.

Across the country, single-DER VPPs are already relieving local grid constraints. In a randomized, controlled pilot with a U.S. utility, ev.energy layered feeder-level dispatch onto an existing managed charging program, and evening dispatch succeeded in every event tested, with no rebound. The technology isn’t the limit; the program design is.

Consider one household across the decade a planner is asked to bank on. In 2027, the household enrolls in the utility’s thermostat program and a leased EV in a managed charging program. In 2029, the lease ends and the new car is a brand the program doesn’t support. In 2031, the family adds a battery and enrolls it in a third program. In 2033, a heat pump and new thermostat replace the furnace. In 2035, a new family moves in with an EV of its own.

The household’s flexibility grew every year. The utility’s programs recorded it as churn, because they were designed around devices, not households, and the devices that remained enrolled were dispatched in silos, not as one VPP resource. As my colleague Nick Woolley has written, operators should plan for about 30% of devices turning over every year. A program built around a fixed roster of siloed devices can relieve this year’s feeder. It can’t promise the same kilowatts in 2035.
articles.lede: Single-device programs treat household change as churn. A portfolio built around households turns it into durable grid capacity.

articles.title: U.S. natural gas inventories end injection season above normal levels
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report and Natural Gas Monthly Note: Five-year average=2021–2025 Working natural gas in storage in the Lower 48 states ended the natural gas injection season at 3,810 billion cubic feet (Bcf), exceeding the five-year average by almost 2%, according to estimates based on data from our Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report released on November 12. Injection season runs April 1–October 31, the months of typically lower natural gas demand.

While net injections were 2 Bcf less than the five-year average this injection season, working gas stocks are higher than usual because they started the 2026 season 3% (63 Bcf) above the five-year average at 1,878 Bcf.

Higher than average inventories at the start of the summer injection season allowed storage operators to reach their end-of-season targets with smaller incremental natural gas injections. Although total dry natural gas production during the 2026 refill season was 3% higher than the same period in 2025, according to S&P Global Energy, most of the increased production during this period was used to meet rising demand from liquefied natural gas export terminals.

Mild spring temperatures during the first several weeks of the refill season mitigated seasonal residential and commercial natural gas demand, allowing the surplus to the five-year average to grow, peaking at 198 Bcf (7%) for the week ending August 7, before declining for the next 10 consecutive weeks, as warmer-than-normal temperatures during the summer months increased power generation demand for natural gas. Mild temperatures returned during the final weeks of the injection season, which led to above-normal injections. Weekly injections ranged from 108 Bcf in early June to 15 Bcf in late August.

In our November Short-Term Energy Outlook, we forecast natural gas withdrawals during the 2026–2027 heating season (November 1–March 31) will total 1,900 Bcf and that inventories will be 4% above the five-year (2022–2026) average at the end of March 2027 because of a relatively mild winter and increases in natural gas production.

Solving the AI data center power bottleneck with superconductors
articles.description: VEIR's Tim Heidel on pivoting from transmission to data centers, cooling cables with liquid nitrogen, and raising a Series C.
paragraphs: Decarbonizing the global economy requires a massive expansion of electrical transmission capacity. But building conventional high-voltage lines often takes over a decade due to local opposition and complex permitting. Tim Heidel, CEO and co-founder of VEIR, initially launched his company to solve this grid problem. His team developed a new generation of high-temperature superconducting cables cooled by liquid nitrogen that have the ability to fit more power into the same physical footprint as traditional copper lines.

Tim’s team also created a system to help meet growing server rack power demands from data centers by condensing dozens of copper wires into a single compact pipe. In addition to saving valuable physical space, the system reduces installation labor by up to eighty percent compared to conventional copper line installation.
Credits: Hosted by Lara Pierpoint. Produced and edited by Ross Kenyon, Anne Bailey, and Stephen Lacey. Sean Marquand is our technical director. Stephen Lacey is our executive editor.

Google signs PPA to buy 50MW geothermal power from Quaise Energy
articles.description: Google has entered into a PPA to acquire 50MW of geothermal energy from Quaise Energy’s Project Obsidian in Central Oregon, US.
paragraphs: Google has entered into a power purchase agreement (PPA) to acquire 50MW of geothermal energy from Quaise Energy’s Project Obsidian in Central Oregon, US.

The agreement is scheduled to begin as early as 2030 and will deliver round-the-clock, carbon-free electricity to Google’s data centre in The Dalles, Oregon, as well as benefiting the wider community.
Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.
Initial development at Project Obsidian will employ conventional drilling techniques to generate superhot geothermal energy at commercial scale.
According to Quaise, this form of geothermal energy can produce up to ten times more electricity per well than standard geothermal systems, as it harnesses much higher temperatures deep underground.
A second phase aims to implement millimetre wave drilling technology, which Quaise says could access superhot geothermal resources in new locations globally.

Quaise Energy CEO and president Carlos Araque said: “We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector.
“Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the US as the global leader in geothermal power.”
From 2010 to 2025, the company signed over 240 deals to buy nearly 35GW of new clean energy, with more than 29GW secured in North America across 148 projects.
Google advanced energy technologies head Lucia Tian said: “Google data centres are long-term investments in the communities we call home.

articles.title: New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant
articles.description: The development in Ann Arbor will share its solar and battery power with the grid, as part of a pilot that aims to lower energy costs and provide…
paragraphs: Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings.
Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid.

In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most.

“ This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil-fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers.

The initiative ​ “ should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​ “ DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, ​ “ a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to spend a lot of time learning and trying to optimize,” he noted. ​ “ DTE will manage that battery for you.” ( DTE did not respond to Canary Media’s request for exact figures on how much it would compensate customers in time for publication.)

VPPs have existed for years but have been slow to gain widespread traction because of a host of factors. Utilities often haven’t been incentivized to embrace the approach, while home solar and batteries remain too expensive for many households in the U.S. But as electrification and the data center rush spur unprecedented demand, VPPs are taking off as a fast way to get power on the grid. Earlier this month, the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources harnessed in VPPs could save households on average $ 122 per year by 2050.
Currently, ​ “ there’s immense untapped capacity,” said Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI.

Matt Grocoff, the founder of Thrive Collaborative, started to consider a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019. He wanted the neighborhood to mimic an ecosystem — a resilient web of relationships in which individual organisms do more than just extract resources. For example, a tree in a forest turns sunlight into nutrients and shares them symbiotically with a vast, interconnected underground web of fungi.

Likewise, with a VPP, each Veridian home ​ “ can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy rather than a linear grid that flows in only one direction,” Grocoff said.

Michigan is a test bed for Democrats’ energy affordability promises
articles.description: Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson and Democratic lawmakers want to tie utility profits to reliability, and pause new data center builds.
paragraphs: Michigan voters handed Democrats a trifecta of state government control after campaigning on promises like cracking down on both utilities and data centers. Now, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson is tasked with turning those promises into actual relief for customers once she takes office in January.

Early next year, lawmakers are expected to release a package of bills aimed at tying utility profits to more reliable and affordable service, as well as scaling up distributed energy resources like community solar and home batteries, clean energy and ratepayer groups told Latitude Media. Some have been introduced before, while others are new.

Meanwhile, given Benson’s campaign promises, they also anticipate the governor-elect will issue a moratorium on new data center construction until the state puts in place guardrails around costs, land and water use, and public disclosures. This would mirror what Gov. Greg Abbott did earlier this year in Texas with executive authority alone, though in Michigan siting is largely decided locally and a construction pause may require the legislature’s buy-in.

Michigan in 2027 will be among nearly two dozen states where Democrats control all three branches of government. But Benson’s agenda specifically will be a key test of whether the party’s energy affordability platform can actually deliver. Michigan is simultaneously trying to achieve 100% clean energy by 2040, upgrade an aging grid, and absorb a wave of new data center demand from hyperscalers including Oracle, Google, and Microsoft — all while limiting rate hikes for customers.

Benson was one of the most aggressive gubernatorial candidates in the country on issues like taking on utilities and data centers, according to Bob Allison, deputy director of the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. “We think she’ll follow through on that and more, especially with the backing of a legislature that ran on these issues,” he told Latitude Media.
A spokeswoman for Benson’s transition team didn’t return requests for comment about how the incoming administration plans to implement its agenda.

Benson pledged to increase bill credits for residents who experience power outages, fund a home energy efficiency program to help lower utility bills, institute performance-based utility profit standards, and ensure residential ratepayers don’t subsidize data centers.

Most of those actions will likely require legislation, said Laura Sherman, president of the Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council. The Michigan Public Service Commission does have an open docket on potential incentives and penalties for utilities aimed at reducing outages and integrating virtual power plants, among other flexible grid resources. However, state law currently limits what the commission can do on its own.

“[MPSC] has also required a number of things related to data centers to ensure costs aren’t passed on to other customers,” Sherman said. “But in terms of clean energy, we haven’t seen the commission require that in certain cases. That is something we’re working on legislatively.”
articles.lede: Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson and Democratic lawmakers want to tie utility profits to reliability, and pause new data center builds.

articles.title: Power sector emissions set to fall in US amid lower coal use
articles.description: Despite record electricity demand and the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up coal, the electricity sector is on track to emit less CO 2 this year…
paragraphs: The U.S. electricity sector is set to emit less planet-warming carbon dioxide this year despite record-high demand and the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up uncompetitive coal-fired power plants.

Power plants burned 10 % less coal through July of this year, according to a new analysis of federal data from think tank Energy Innovation. That drop in coal consumption caused power sector emissions to decline in the first half of 2026 — and puts the U.S. on track for a 2 % reduction in overall energy-related emissions across this entire year.

It’s a reversal from 2025, when coal generation shot up 13 % and caused economy-wide emissions to jump 2. 4 %. Analysts attributed that to a surge in electricity demand coupled with unusually high natural gas prices, which made coal more economically attractive.
This year, though, coal plants are just not running as often. Through August 2026, coal plants ran an average of 46. 7 % of the time, compared with 49. 7 % over the same period last year.
The data suggests that coal’s resurgence last year was a blip rather than the start of a boom, even as electricity demand has continued to soar this year.

Coal’s decline is particularly notable because the White House has employed aggressive and at times extralegal means to boost the fuel, which pollutes the air and water with mercury and other toxins while also emitting more carbon dioxide than other power sources.

The Department of Energy has been ordering coal plants to stay open past their planned retirement dates on the grounds of an alleged energy crisis. These orders have burdened consumers with hundreds of millions of dollars in costs, despite some of the plants being too run-down to produce any power. The DOE also announced hundreds of millions of dollars in funding coal plants, while the Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back regulations on pollution from the facilities.

Around 48 gigawatts of coal capacity shuttered in Trump’s first term, far more than in either of President Barack Obama’s terms in the White House. Last year saw a far smaller amount of coal retirements, and so this year, the fleet has shrunk by only 1. 6 %. It now stands at about 167. 5 GW, said report author Robbie Orvis, Energy Innovation’s senior director of modeling and analysis.
But just because old coal plants are sticking around, it doesn’t mean that they’re contributing more to the energy system.

What else is picking up the slack? Not combined-cycle gas turbines, the large-format workhorses of the electricity sector. Through August, they ran at a slightly lower rate than they did last year. Overall gas consumption at power plants did tick up 3. 8 %, however, indicating greater production from different types of gas facilities, like peaker plants, for example.
articles.lede: The U.S. electricity sector is set to emit less planet-warming carbon dioxide this year despite record-high demand and the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up uncompetitive coal-fired power plants.

articles.title: Google bets on superhot geothermal to power Oregon data centers
articles.description: The tech giant inked a $500M-plus deal to secure clean power from Quaise Energy, a geothermal startup developing rock-melting beams for its first…
paragraphs: The geothermal startup Quaise Energy has landed a major first customer for its novel, superhot project in central Oregon.

On Tuesday, the Houston-based firm announced that Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of carbon-free power from Quaise’s first commercial project, called Project Obsidian, near the Newberry Volcano. Quaise will deploy advanced drilling techniques and unique rock-melting technology to access significantly hotter geothermal resources than traditional plants can.
Google said it plans to use the energy to help run its existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030.
The deal is valued at more than $ 500 million, Quaise confirmed. The startup is working to find offtakers for an additional 200 MW in future capacity at the Oregon site.

“ We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector,” Carlos Araque, Quaise’s CEO and president, said in a Tuesday statement.

Quaise is one of at least four U.S. geothermal companies to land agreements with tech giants to pursue next-generation plants. Fervo Energy, the startup that’s furthest along in project development, recently inked a landmark deal to supply Google with nearly 400 MW of clean electricity from the Cape Station facility in southwest Utah. Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy are both partnering with Meta to develop facilities in Nevada and New Mexico, respectively.

Tech firms are seeking to secure sources of clean, around-the-clock power for their vast buildout of data centers. For geothermal startups, winning customer contracts like these is an essential step toward raising the financing they need to build first-of-a-kind facilities. Their technologies, while promising, have yet to be deployed widely at commercial scales — and questions remain about how effectively they’ll be able to operate over long periods of time.

Google is investing in other nascent technologies, too, including long-duration energy storage and advanced nuclear power. ​ “ The scale of power that we’re looking for and also the scale of impact we’re trying to have on the grid requires us to foster that ecosystem,” Lucia Tian, who leads Google’s advanced energy technologies team, told the Wall Street Journal.

Quaise said its Oregon project will cost about $ 350 million to build. The company raised $ 180 million in equity financing in August, which included investment from the oil-and-gas drilling firm Nabors Industries. (Another startup, Mazama Energy, recently nabbed $ 135 million to accelerate its own superhot geothermal project near the Newberry Volcano.)

At the Project Obsidian site, Quaise will initially use oil-and-gas drilling technologies to develop an enhanced geothermal system. The emerging approach involves fracturing rocks and pumping them full of water to create artificial reservoirs. Surrounding rocks heat the water, which is used to drive turbines on the surface to produce power.
articles.lede: The geothermal startup Quaise Energy has landed a major first customer for its novel, superhot project in central Oregon.
