articles.title: Are distributed data centers the answer to AI’s power crunch?
articles.description: The case for smaller data centers is getting stronger.
paragraphs: We’ve been sold a very specific story about AI data centers: bigger is always better. But is that true?
There’s no question that we need a lot more computation to push the limits of large language models. But there’s a new debate emerging around how it should get built.

Over the last year, distributed computing has gained attention as a possible solution to the challenges facing data centers. They’re being framed as a way to avoid costly grid upgrades, reduce local opposition, use empty office buildings, and even give homeowners a financial stake in AI.

It’s turning into a distributed energy story. Companies like Span, Sunrun, Arcadia, and Generate Capital are exploring residential and commercial compute nodes paired with solar and batteries. Others, like Perimeter, are turning old office buildings into data centers.
So far, the market is very small. But what would it take to scale these models? And are there hidden impacts on the grid that we need to consider?
Plus, we talk about the fallout from Jensen Huang’s departure from NVIDIA, and explore some storylines in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections.

Open Circuit is brought to you by EnergyHub. EnergyHub works with more than 230 utilities to coordinate over 2.6 million DERs and more than 3.6 gigawatts of dispatchable flexibility through a single platform designed to perform when it counts most. See what that looks like at EnergyHub.com.

Open Circuit is brought to you by Everyday Electric. Everyday Electric simplifies savings at home, helping support a more reliable, affordable grid. Operating the country’s largest residential VPP, it coordinates 6+ GW of capacity across connected products. Learn more at everydayelectric.com.

Stephen Lacey: In 2017, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, then a researcher at OpenAI, wrote a memo that set today’s infrastructure boom in motion. It was called “The Big Blob of Compute.” It argued that the only way to build general-purpose AI was to make the models bigger. Clever, narrow models were not the answer, he argued. Rather, it was more compute, more data, and longer training runs. That research hypothesis became the operating philosophy of leading AI companies, and the blob grew into something physical: gigawatt-scale campuses, nuclear restarts, gas plants, big batteries, and a build-out now measured in the trillions of dollars. We’ve been told a very specific story about the direction of AI infrastructure: bigger is always better. But is it? There’s no question that we need way more computing to push the frontier of general-purpose models. But large data centers face so much opposition and so many constraints that there’s a debate over how that computing gets built.

Should it — can it — be far more distributed? Rather than taking up thousands of acres, could the computing live in smaller warehouses, empty office space, or even homes? This week, we’ll look at emerging models for distributed computing and how they’re becoming a distributed energy play. Plus, we’ll dip back into some post-midterm commentary and talk about the fallout from Jensen Huang’s departure from NVIDIA. That’s coming right up on Open Circuit.
articles.lede: The case for smaller data centers is getting stronger.

How does EIA account for small differences between energy supply and demand data?
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Note: Supply = production + imports; demand = consumption + exports; demand - supply = stock change + other EIA uses over 60 surveys to collect data on the U.S. energy sector’s supply and demand. In theory, supply and demand should balance. In practice, we often have small differences between our total supply and total demand figures.

To account for the differences between U.S. total primary energy supply and demand, our Monthly Energy Review includes a stock change and other data series, a grouping of items that account for the differences between supply and demand each month.

These accounting differences represent a very small share of energy markets. In 2025, our combined surveys accounted for about 128 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) each for U.S. energy supply and demand, and stock change and other was 0.4 quads—about 0.3% of the total.
Stock change is the net difference between energy held in storage at the beginning and end of a month.

The other portion of stock change and other represents the many forms of small accounting differences: Differences in survey respondent accounting and reporting practices Differences in timing between energy activity occurrences and reporting periods Measurement and estimation errors Limitations in data collection systems and survey coverage Energy lost during transfers or storage Unreported energy activities

To document the other differences between supply and demand, besides stock change, we use various adjustments, balancing items, and losses and unaccounted for series, a standard statistical accounting practice. Rather than indicating a flaw in the underlying statistics, these series ensure that published data are consistent and transparent, while also providing a measure of the uncertainty associated with our survey data.

For petroleum and biofuels, our adjustments series accounts for the fact that survey responses may not precisely reflect actual activity. We’ve made improvements to our petroleum data over time to account for changes in transfers to crude oil supply, motor gasoline blending components, distillate fuel oil by pipeline operations, and other developments in petroleum markets. See Appendix B of our Petroleum Supply Monthly for more details.

For natural gas, our balancing item series accounts for differences between supply and demand. Some of the differences are because of natural gas lost to the atmosphere. Also, there can be differences in conversions of flow data metered at varying temperatures and pressures, variations in company accounting and billing practices, and differences between billing cycles and calendar periods. See Appendix A of our Natural Gas Monthly for more details.

For coal, we use a losses and unaccounted for series to represent differences in supply and demand, including coal lost during transport and various accounting and timing issues. In 2009, because of incomplete data coverage and different source data, biofuels have a small balancing item to balance biodiesel supply and demand.

Inside Moment Energy’s new battery system for C&I customers
articles.description: Exclusive: The company is betting FEOC-compliance and safety are the answer to scaling second-life EV battery deployments.
paragraphs: As the price of new batteries falls, companies repurposing used electric vehicle packs have faced a tricky math problem: Do the savings on batteries themselves outweigh the work of assessing, integrating, certifying, and deploying packs with different histories?

Moment Energy, a Canadian battery maker, is betting its new system can balance that equation for commercial and industrial sites — especially in a moment when U.S. buyers are weighing the value of federal tax credits against the cost of meeting foreign entity sourcing restrictions. According to CEO Edward Chiang, using batteries that are already in circulation avoids both the cost and logistical headache of purchasing new cells via a China-dependent supply chain.

Chiang said Moment’s systems are 30% cheaper than Chinese alternatives even before tax credits, with savings reaching as high as 70% when incentives are included. Preserving that advantage, however, depends on keeping integration, installation, and pack replacement costs low.

In addition to cost-competitiveness, Moment is pitching compactness and safety qualifications as advantages for deployments at places like hospitals, airports, and manufacturing facilities. Moment’s new stationary storage system, dubbed Nova, is roughly the size of a parking spot, and has a power rating of 200 kilowatts and an energy capacity of 500 kilowatt-hours — enough to discharge at full power for two hours. Chiang said Nova is the first fully UL-certified BESS made with repurposed EV batteries on the market. That certification, he added, is a critical differentiator for the company, because it supports deployments close to buildings, making the compact system an option for space-constrained commercial and urban sites.

It’s the combination of Moment’s battery management system and power electronics that allow Nova to accommodate packs with different chemistries, architectures, and states of health, Chiang said. Those controls also allow the company to replace individual modules, rather than scrap an entire container when something goes wrong.

The battery recycling industry has so far struggled to truly scale, in part because there just aren’t enough used batteries to go around. But Chiang isn’t concerned that Moment will run into those challenges.
Chiang estimates there’s around 300 gigawatt-hours of potential feedstock available today, which will grow 950 GWh by 2030. Those numbers are based on EVs sold 15 years ago, he explained.

Moment is currently planning for two GWh of annual capacity at its to-be-built factory in Austin, and 2.2 megawatt-hours at its factory in Vancouver. At that rate, Chiang said Moment could succeed with only a fraction of the battery supply expected to become available.
A slowdown in EV sales, which Chiang attributed in part to changes in federal tax credits, “is actually quite good from a waste perspective, because it now allows companies like us to catch up.”
“When I’m repurposing 2 GWh per year…most of those batteries still end up in landfills, which is not good,” he added.
articles.lede: Exclusive: The company is betting FEOC-compliance and safety are the answer to scaling second-life EV battery deployments.

In the South, heat pumps are the secret to a more reliable grid
articles.description: Much of the region uses the equivalent of an “electric hair dryer” to heat their homes — and it creates big problems for the grid. Heat pumps could help.
paragraphs: For many in North Carolina and Tennessee, 2022’s Winter Storm Elliott lives in infamy. Temperatures plunged well below freezing for days at a time, just as families were gathered at home for the Christmas holiday. The grid couldn’t keep up, and some 1. 6 million households lost power in rolling blackouts in those two states alone.

Like Winter Storm Uri in Texas the year before, Elliott was generally understood as a problem of supply: Scores of power plants, mostly gas-burning, failed because of frozen equipment. To maintain future reliability during bitter cold weather, regulators recommended that utilities winter-proof their gas plants and diversify by building more power sources.

But the authors of a new report say that increasing supply isn’t the cheapest way to prevent future winter blackouts across the U.S. South. Instead, the best option is reducing demand — specifically, from the old-fashioned, energy-sucking electric resistance furnaces that are more common in this region of the country than any other.

“ Across the 14 states that we looked at in this analysis, there are approximately 8 million households that essentially heat their house with an electric hair dryer,” said Alex Antal, a report co-author and principal at the Regulatory Assistance Project, a global clean energy nonprofit.

If these homes instead covered most of their heating needs with heat pumps, which are three times more efficient than electric resistance furnaces, it would drastically reduce systemwide electricity demand — and utility bills. In fact, the report finds that heat pump deployment in the region would save as much power as that produced by 100 ​ “ peaker” plants, which are dispatched only when demand climbs high enough and are among the most expensive units on the grid. Building and maintaining new plants to create the same amount of electricity would cost six to nine times more, the report concludes.

“ Those power plants are otherwise sitting unused the rest of the year,” said Forest Bradley-Wright, a report co-author and the state and utility program director at the nonprofit American Council for an Energy Efficient Economy. Improving home-heating efficiency, he said, ​ “ avoids the need to build more power plants that we all have to pay for. That saves money for everyone.”

The households that install heat pumps would save the most. The report identifies homes best suited to do this: those that have outdated electric heaters and central air conditioning. It calculates the benefits for customers who invest in heat pumps — which both cool and heat homes — when their AC reaches the end of its useful life. It assumes the existing electric furnace will remain as a backup.

A whole-home heat pump on average costs about $ 560 more than a traditional whole-home air conditioner, according to the report. But because it’s so much more efficient, the heat pump will cut annual electricity bills by $ 250, and pay for itself in about three years. Over 15 years, the cumulative savings across the entire region are estimated at nearly $ 30 billion — compared with a total investment of about $ 4. 8 billion.
articles.lede: Much of the region uses the equivalent of an “electric hair dryer” to heat their homes — and it creates big problems for the grid.

articles.title: New international energy storage alliance launched at COP31
articles.description: A new international platform aimed at enhancing cooperation on energy storage was launched at the China Pavilion during COP31.
paragraphs: A new international platform, named the Global Energy Storage Alliance (GESA), aimed at enhancing cooperation on energy storage was launched at the China Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

The GESA initiative was established through the joint efforts of the China Energy Storage Alliance (CNESA), China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage Co. and the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute (CREEI), together with additional industry stakeholders.
Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.
The alliance seeks to address the role of energy storage in power-system flexibility and renewable energy integration as countries accelerate their adoption of clean energy sources.

Senior officials attending the launch included Li Gao, China’s Vice Minister of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, and Xiong Minfeng, Deputy Director-General of the Department of International Cooperation of the National Energy Administration of China.

Also present were Francesco La Camera, Director-General of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), and Selwin Hart, Special Adviser to the UN Secretary-General on Climate Action and Just Transition.
The event took place during a side meeting focused on digital-intelligent innovation and green electricity.

GESA was introduced amid mounting challenges faced by the sector, such as energy security concerns, varying technical standards across countries, and gaps in financing and business models, particularly in emerging markets.

CREEI International Cooperation Department director, lead scientist and director-general assistant Dr Jiang Hao, stated that the initiative aims to promote large-scale, diversified, and innovation-driven energy storage around the world. The goal is to position storage as a central part of new power systems through international collaboration and support the global energy transition and climate efforts.

CNESA secretary-general Liu Wei outlined six priority areas for GESA: facilitating global dialogue, developing databases and standards, advancing technology deployment, fostering business model innovation, enhancing supply-chain coordination, and supporting investment and project cooperation.
articles.lede: A new international platform aimed at enhancing cooperation on energy storage was launched at the China Pavilion during COP31.

articles.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
articles.description: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.
paragraphs: Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.
Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO.
It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.
Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.
There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.
Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions, the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.
This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.
This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño. However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.
articles.lede: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

articles.title: Texas data centers are staring down a December limbo
articles.description: The Batch Zero process just got a lot less clear.
paragraphs: It’s going to be a strange winter for Texas data center developers, and for the companies betting on providing them with power. They were already waiting to hear the results of Gov. Greg Abbott’s data center audit, which stopped approving grid connections for new data centers and crypto mines of 75 megawatts or more until regulators have the chance to review them.

So far, ERCOT has provisionally let some 200 projects totaling 66.4 gigawatts keep their place in line, and has already shut out over 350 projects totaling more than 300 GW. That leaves nearly 170 GW worth of projects still waiting for the Texas green light, according to a Latitude Intelligence analysis of the queue.

Clarity on the review process, known as “Batch Zero,” has long been expected in December. But then Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the election for governor, ending the GOP’s 30-year run in the governor’s mansion, and raising questions about how and if she’ll maintain Gov. Abbott’s plans.

The state is the second-largest data center market in the U.S., and in her campaign, Hinojosa blamed Abbott for that explosive growth; Abbott just a year ago declared Texas the “epicenter of AI development,” and offered incentives for qualifying data centers looking to build in the state. Hinojosa said she would block new construction until state lawmakers can pass stronger restrictions, including on water and energy use. She takes office on January 19, 2027.

Of course, Hinojosa can’t do everything on her own. Passing laws like Senate Bill 6, which rewrote the rules for how large loads connect to and operate on the grid, requires lawmaker cooperation — and after Democrats also took the statehouse this month, 2027 will be the first time in 25 years that there will be a partisan split in the legislature. But her predecessor froze the load queue via letters to the Public Utilities Commission, ERCOT, and the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, which means that Hinojosa can do the same.

Analysts for the investment bank Jefferies said in a post-election note that they’re skeptical that the new governor will reverse changes already implemented by Abbott. Instead, they anticipate that “the most plausible policy outcome is a legislative compromise that codifies consumer protections and sets guardrails on large-scale development.”
“The pause could be long,” they added, though they “expect Texas to build significant data centers in 2028 [and beyond]. Those already underway appear to be accelerating.”

The reasoning behind the Abbott pause, as well as Hinojosa’s stated plans, includes concerns about whether data centers are driving up costs for ratepayers. But because of the peculiarities of the Texas market, the absence of new data centers could also have a direct impact on prices, both for consumers and for power producers. Wholesale power for future years already trades at prices that assume, according to Jefferies, about six GW of grid-connected data centers each year. If those facilities don’t arrive, those prices fall. That is good for bills, and bad for the companies that own power plants.
articles.lede: The Batch Zero process just got a lot less clear.

articles.title: Permitting reform is a big, controversial bet for the energy transition
articles.description: Clean energy backers say the bill would boost renewables and the power grid more than it would help fossil fuels. Some environmentalists fear they’re dead…
paragraphs: The Senate bipartisan permitting bill is essentially an enormous three-part bet by the Democrats and clean energy advocates who support it.

The first part of the bet is that streamlining federal environmental reviews and permitting processes for all energy infrastructure will lead to more clean than dirty energy getting built, because renewables are cheaper and faster to get up and running.

The second is that the Trump administration will follow through on commitments to stop blocking clean energy — and that it won’t take advantage of the changes to fast-track a bunch of dirty projects that a future administration would struggle to overturn.
The third is that there will not be a better opportunity to initiate reforms that must be put in place for the economy to successfully decarbonize.

Not everyone thinks these bets will pay off for the climate. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which the Senate is expected to vote on this week, has sown divisions between some historic allies for decarbonization policy.

Influential climate groups including the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Sierra Club, and the Union of Concerned Scientists have come out against the bill over concerns that it will make it too easy to build new fossil fuel infrastructure. After all, the American Petroleum Institute is one of the bill’s backers, and the Trump administration — as clear a friend to fossil fuels and foe to clean energy as there is — has given its blessing to the current version.

But many climate policy advocates and analysts contend that the bill is a clear positive for the energy transition. BAAJA was co-written by Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, two of clean energy’s loudest supporters in Congress. It has broad support: Clean energy industry groups, labor unions, and some previously on-the-fence environmental organizations have come out in favor of it.
“ Let’s make it possible for America to build big things in this country again,” Heinrich said during a press conference with Whitehouse and other supporters last week.

The core contention of BAAJA backers is that the barriers to clean energy are no longer financial — they’re institutional. Decades of policies designed to protect the public and the environment from harmful infrastructure development, including fossil fuel pipelines and power plants, have become barriers to building the things needed to decarbonize.

“ Financial incentives only work if the things it makes financial sense to build can get permitted,” said Jesse Jenkins, an associate professor and energy systems engineer at Princeton University. ​ “ If we can’t build clean energy infrastructure at speed and scale, we can’t decarbonize the United States economy.”
articles.lede: The Senate bipartisan permitting bill is essentially an enormous three-part bet by the Democrats and clean energy advocates who support it.

articles.title: Voltus buys Stem storage platform as it doubles down on batteries
articles.description: Exclusive: The sale comes as the VPP company expands its BYOC offering for data centers — and launches a new BESS coalition.
paragraphs: Virtual power plant provider Voltus is angling to get more energy storage involved in flexible demand management, including via the purchase of a distributed battery optimization and management platform called Athena, built by Stem.

Larsh Johnson, chief technology officer at Voltus, exclusively told Latitude Media that the platform will allow Voltus to accelerate its strategy to add more battery energy storage to its existing virtual power plant work. “We have to have more batteries under management,” Johnson said. “If we can provide battery flex, we can actually deliver the kind of capacity that our partners really need.”

Athena is another example of the same. According to the company, Athena weighs a range of factors such as real-time market signals, utility tariffs, weather, and grid constraints “to dispatch batteries automatically, manage peak loads and optimize revenue per megawatt.” Because a battery functions as both a generator and a load, Johnson added, Voltus needs a tailored monitoring and control system to best incorporate them into a VPP.

“That complements how you take that kind of battery-specific functionality into the market by managing the battery’s energy and being able to optimize it for dispatch under the conditions where a customer is saving money on their utility bill and ensuring that the available energy is used in the best way possible,” he said.

Voltus was the original pioneer of BYOC, which lets data centers leverage surrounding commercial and industrial power flexibility rather than reducing their own energy use as they would in a standard demand response agreement. The concept is now getting picked up by those in the residential space as well, including Sunrun, Tesla, and Everyday Electric.
Johnson knows the Athena system well because he worked at Stem when the company developed the platform. He then left Stem to join Brightfield AI before its acquisition by Voltus.
Johnson said the Athena platform has hosted hundreds of batteries operating around the country, “so we know we’re acquiring a proven platform.”

Also today, Voltus launched a network of battery energy storage companies that are working together to accelerate the deployment of flexible grid capacity. The nearly 40 member companies include Branch Energy, Scale Microgrids, and Sparkfund. The network will connect commercial and industrial customers with assistance on engineering, permitting, construction, financing, and battery development partners.
Houston-based Stem has provided energy asset monitoring products for nearly 20 years, and its integrated software suite, PowerTrack, is commonly used in the industry.

I’m still feeling melancholy about leaving Denmark. Read about tryg, the Danish sense of relaxed safety that comes with a high-trust culture. Sure sounds better than the constant low-level sense of threat and anxiety that seems to dominate in the US. (According to Google, “tryg” is the adjective (safe, secure) and “tryghed” is the noun, the feeling. But nobody likes a pedant.)

articles.title: Could a data center’s waste heat warm a North Carolina town?
articles.description: Enfield wants a proposed data center to fund community benefits, including a thermal energy network that would use its excess heat — it’d be a first for…
paragraphs: In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs.

Voters didn’t just take their anger out on politicians. In red and blue areas alike, they also approved dozens of ballot measures pausing or restricting data centers, adding to the over 450 moratoriums already in place across the country.
The backlash has left state and local leaders grappling with how to put guardrails on the facilities and ensure they benefit nearby communities.

A forthcoming deal between a data center and Enfield, North Carolina — an overwhelmingly poor, majority Black town of 2, 000 — could offer a groundbreaking example of what such development might look like.

For years, Enfield leaders and their allies have been working toward a clean energy vision that includes a solar farm to supply residents with power, a new substation to help distribute those renewable electrons, and a thermal energy network — a shallow form of geothermal that could replace inefficient water heating, space heating, and cooling. But they’ve faced a dearth of funding and fierce policy headwinds under President Donald Trump.

Then, this summer, Halifax County, where Enfield sits, announced it was selling property to Wyoming-based Quiet Data Centers, a land development firm, for a 100, 000 square-foot facility. The industrial site is 2 miles outside the town but needs to tap into its wastewater systems.

For Enfield Mayor Mondale Robinson, that presented a bargaining opportunity. Now, he and top officials from Quiet are negotiating a community benefits agreement, a legally binding document that ties developers to certain benchmarks. Among other commitments, Robinson wants the company to fund the entire $ 16. 2 million clean energy plan.

What’s more, he wants the data center to join the thermal energy network, which could provide a surge of excess heat to meet the whole town’s needs. If the plans come to fruition, it would be the first time in the U.S. that a data center has connected to such a system.

Brendan Morris, Quiet’s chief development officer, confirmed to Canary Media that the discussions were ongoing and that all of Enfield’s aims were on the table. ​ “ I think things are possible,” he said. ​ “ We’re new to this community and new to the county. We look around and see how a new business and a new data center coming into the area can make a positive impact.”

Robinson, a self-proclaimed progressive, acknowledges that the midterms were a rebuke of the tech sector’s buildout. ​ “ Everybody should be against dirty data centers,” he said. But he believes the not-in-my-backyard approach has too often stuck communities like Enfield with polluting projects rejected by wealthier areas. That’s why he wants a data center that’s built sustainably and with community input. ​ “ There’s nothing progressive about saying we are against something, without saying what we are for,” he added.

articles.title: A year in, New England heat pump program is thriving
articles.description: The five-state New England Heat Pump Accelerator is just getting started, but supporters think it will meet a goal of nearly 580,000 heat pumps installed…
paragraphs: More than 25, 000 homes across New England will be keeping warm this winter with new energy-efficient, low-emission systems paid for, in part, by federal funds. The households are participants in a five-state effort to boost cold-climate heat pump adoption that launched one year ago this month.

While that is well short of the ultimate goal of nearly 580, 000 heat pumps installed in four years, the growth of the program — the New England Heat Pump Accelerator — in its first months has supporters feeling confident about its chances for success.

“ We’re very, very optimistic about this goal,” said Ellen Pfeiffer, a fellow with Energy Solutions, a clean energy consultancy that is helping implement the programming, during a webinar last week reviewing the program’s first year. ​ “ We see vastly more participation just with these added incentives.”

The accelerator — a joint endeavor between Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island — is backed by $ 450 million from the federal Climate Pollution Reduction Grants program, which was created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. It was, and remains, a rare example of a major Biden-era initiative making headway despite the Trump administration’s relentless efforts to eliminate federal clean energy and environmental funding.

New England is particularly well poised to take advantage of heat pumps because of its current reliance on fossil fuels. More than half the single-family homes in Connecticut, Maine, and New Hampshire use heating oil, as do large portions of those in Massachusetts and Rhode Island. Propane and natural gas are also in wide use.

Switching to a heat pump yields substantial monthly bill savings for most oil customers and a significant portion of propane and natural gas users. It also cuts climate-warming pollution: The only emissions associated with heat pumps are those produced by generating the electricity needed to operate the systems.

“ It’s the closest thing we have to a magic trick in the energy industry,” said Andy Frank, deputy commissioner of energy and technology policy at the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.

The accelerator program is slated to last four years, but it aims to leave behind a permanently transformed market in which accessible prices, readily available equipment, and a well-trained workforce make heat pumps the default choice for home heating well into the future. The long-term goal is for heat pumps to make up 90 % of heating system sales in the region by 2040.
“ We are shifting what is bought and sold in the market,” said Dylan Voorhees, managing consultant at nonprofit clean energy advisory VEIC, an implementation partner.

The centerpiece of the effort is the midstream incentive. Distributors — the plumbing and equipment supply companies that sell to contractors — receive an incentive payment for selling cold-climate heat pumps and heat pump water heaters. They get to keep a small sum, and the rest is passed on to the buyer as a discount: $ 300 incentive for heat-pump water heaters and $ 650 for space-heating heat pumps in four states. Maine has chosen to concentrate its program exclusively on heat-pump water heaters, using the accelerator money to fund its existing incentives.
articles.lede: More than 25, 000 homes across New England will be keeping warm this winter with new energy-efficient, low-emission systems paid for, in part, by federal funds.

How California Gov.-elect Becerra could be better on climate than Newsom
articles.description: Leah Stokes joined me at a Canary event to talk about her hopes for Xavier Becerra, school electrification, California climate politics, and more.
paragraphs: Welcome back, everyone! Well, we may have finally caught a break when it comes to making progress on climate and energy. The midterm elections have given Democrats control of Congress and dramatically expanded the party’s power in state legislatures and governors’ mansions. That’s opening up big opportunities for reinvigorated clean — and affordable — energy transition policies and actions across the country.

In California, Canary Media just held what amounts to a big party for Golden State climate and energy aficionados: our fourth annual Canary Live Bay Area show, which brought nearly 400 people to The Freight in downtown Berkeley on Tuesday night. The vibe was fantastic — with so much exuberance at the blue wave lifting our common climate ambitions. And onstage and off, there was a whole bunch of gritty, detail-oriented discussion about how to best proceed on all the work ahead.

I was thrilled to share the stage with Leah Stokes, the Anton Vonk Associate Professor of Environmental Politics at the University of California, Santa Barbara; author of top-ranked climate books ​ “ Short Circuiting Policy” and the newly released ​ “ The Carbon Wave”; writer of the Substack ​ “ Notes from the Electric Era”; and one of the chief behind-the-scenes architects of the Biden-era climate triumph, the Inflation Reduction Act. She even created a Carbon Wave Calculator to help people understand how to make climate progress in their communities.

Stokes has a lot to say about outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom’s climate and environmental justice policy record — much of it not very flattering. She’s particularly angry that Newsom clawed back nearly $ 200 million in funding for schools to upgrade their heating, air-conditioning, ventilation, and plumbing systems — a move he made right when schools in Santa Barbara were reporting classroom temperatures of 93 degrees Fahrenheit. ​ “ Half a million kids were under extreme heat-modified days at the same time that Gov. Newsom gutted that program,” she said.

She and I eventually turned to Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra’s potential climate agenda. She, for one, is feeling hopeful. ​ “ I think that there’s more of a focus on affordability, on holding the utilities accountable, on delivering on environmental justice,” she said. ​ “ I think that these are things that actually matter to Becerra.”

In particular, she’s a fan of Becerra’s free ​ “ Power Hour” proposal for no-cost utility power when solar is flooding the state’s grid — an idea that’s been pioneered in Australia and floated for California by Stokes herself and a number of other climate thinkers.

For more than a decade, California has been trying to design energy policy to solve for the ​ “ duck curve” — excess solar at midday, not enough grid power as the sun goes down. Batteries can soak up that power, obviously. But so can heat pumps and air conditioners that preheat or precool homes and buildings, as can heat-pump water heaters, which store energy in tanks of hot water, she said.
articles.lede: Leah Stokes joined me at a Canary event to talk about her hopes for Xavier Becerra, school electrification, California climate politics, and more.

‘Electrify everything’ hits the global stage
articles.description: The world gets most of its power from fossil fuels. Mass electrification, promoted by this year’s climate conference, is still a climate solution.
paragraphs: World leaders — well, some of them — gathered in Turkey this week for COP 31, the annual climate conference, for discussions focused on how we power our world. Specifically, conference organizers proposed that attendees join in on a goal of meeting 35 % of the world’s final energy demand with electricity by 2035, up from just over 20 % today.

Achieving that target demands participation from across the global economy. Everyday drivers and shippers will need to replace gasoline- and diesel-powered cars and trucks with plug-in alternatives. Manufacturers will need to swap in industrial heat pumps and electric boilers. Steel and ironmakers must embrace electric arc furnaces and other cleaner technologies.

But if the power that supplies all those electric vehicles, heat pumps, and furnaces comes from fossil fuels, will electrification still make a dent in global emissions? Yes, and there are a few reasons why.

For one, electrification is a necessary step to ditching fossil fuels. And it can take a long time to make the switch, whether it’s your home’s heating or an industrial-scale system providing steam to a factory. Getting more homes and processes electrified now means a larger portion of the world’s energy demand will be cleaned up as soon as more renewables arrive on the grid.

Electric-powered machines are also way more energy efficient than fossil-fueled options, as energy and climate policy expert Jan Rosenow has explained. A lot of energy gets wasted when you burn fossil fuels, particularly in small localized applications like a boiler that heats up a home. But you can get the same result with less fuel — and fewer carbon emissions — if you burn natural gas at a big power plant and then use that electricity to power a heat pump.

Electrification has a benefit beyond emissions, too — one that has become especially pertinent as the war in the Middle East has sent global oil and gas prices through the roof. It lets countries reduce their reliance on imported fossil fuels.

In Europe and Asia, people have responded by buying electric stoves and cars to curb their reliance on imported oil and natural gas. And the EU, learning both from the Iran war and the ongoing struggle in Ukraine, announced plans in July to ramp up electricity’s share of energy use to 46 % by 2040.
Whatever comes out of this year’s COP meeting, expect these climate, efficiency, and security benefits to keep nudging countries toward ever-greater levels of electrification.

The Senate’s bipartisan permitting bill passed its first big test this week as legislators voted 73 - 25 to formally take up the proposal. The bill as written would speed up permitting timelines for transmission, clean energy, and fossil fuel projects, but it’s likely to undergo a lot of edits before it becomes law.

Monday’s vote was the Senate’s first since Election Day, when it became clear Democrats would have resounding majorities in both houses of Congress next year. Many Democratic senators voted against advancing the permitting bill, with some saying they could use their newfound power to beef up the legislation’s clean energy benefits — and address concerns that the bill is too generous to fossil fuel interests.

articles.title: Hydropower generation in the Southwest fell to record lows this summer
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923, Power Plant Operating Data Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey.

Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows.

However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years.

We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity.
According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region's generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.

Solar PAC got revenge on clean energy’s enemies in Congress
articles.description: Most of the GOP lawmakers targeted by the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition lost reelection. The PAC is now looking toward 2028.
paragraphs: Before this election cycle, it was hard to identify any politician who feared the solar industry. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC set out to change that, and now has a roster of wins to back up its threats.

The super PAC, funded and led by solar entrepreneurs and investors, emerged during the midterm primaries with pledges to spend millions of dollars on attack ads against politicians who undermined clean energy policy. ITC got the outcomes it wanted in all six primaries it targeted. Its ads didn’t mention renewables, but instead used messages that tested well with voters — for instance blasting archconservative members of Congress for not being MAGA enough.

In the general election, ITC engaged in 17 congressional races, many of them in districts that President Donald Trump won by double digits, said Tom Matzzie, who chairs the PAC. ITC saw its desired outcome in 13 of those races, counting the apparent, though not totally final, loss by Republican Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4 th District. ITC’s targets won election in four cases: Arizona’s 2 nd District, Florida’s 13 th, Florida’s 27 th, and New York’s 21 st.

“ We definitely sent a message that we can make an impact no matter where you are,” Matzzie said. Of the Republicans who signed a letter in May 2025 calling to ​ “ fully repeal” the Inflation Reduction Act, 40 % won’t be returning to their jobs in Congress.
The PAC lost its perfect hit rate, but after spending $ 17 million across the election cycle, it’s on track for 19 wins out of 23 races, or 83 % success.

ITC wasn’t solely responsible for all Republican losses. The group exploited a political environment that had soured on unified GOP control of Washington, amid rising costs, an open-ended war in Iran that disrupted the global energy trade, novel and highly lucrative forms of corruption, and masked federal operatives attacking immigrants and citizens alike in the streets of American cities.

But the group demonstrated a knack for homing in on its targets’ weaknesses and amplifying them to voters who might not have gotten the message otherwise. The PAC also frequently trolled the candidates to get under their skin. After the election, the group issued press statements calling Brandon Herrera, who lost in Texas’ 23 rd, ​ “ one of the most despicable candidates we’ve ever seen run for office,” and saying of the incumbent in New Jersey’s 2 nd, ​ “ Jeff Van Drew always looked out for Jeff Van Drew, and now he can do it full time.”

In several races, ITC’s targets ended up corroborating the group’s effectiveness, by giving interviews venting about how the PAC was making reelection harder for them. Boebert recently guest-hosted ​ “ The Matt Gaetz Show” — a conservative talk show — and spent some of that time in the spotlight criticizing the solar PAC for obscuring its true policy aim behind ads on other topics.

To maximize its impact, the PAC deliberately chose races where promising Democratic candidates weren’t getting much outside funding. It became the biggest spender in Indiana’s 5 th District, dropping more money on ads than either candidate’s campaign mustered. After the Republican lost, the group released a braggadocious statement to the press: ​ “ Tell Victoria Spartz. We want her to know it was us.”

articles.title: The Iran war will cause global fossil fuel emissions to fall
articles.description: Counter to analysts’ early expectations, planet-warming pollution from fossil fuels is set to dip in 2026 — the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic.
paragraphs: This time it was not plague but war driving the decline. The Iran war has caused brutal increases in oil and natural gas prices, leading many countries to cut their consumption of the fossil fuels and seek alternatives.

It’s not an especially large drop. Fossil-fuel-related emissions will tick down by less than half a percent this year, compared to 2025, per new data from the Global Carbon Project. Nevertheless, it’s a surprising development: Analysts had initially expected emissions to rise this year.
It was clear from the earliest days that the Iran war would reshape the world’s energy use.

Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 25 % of the world’s crude oil and 19 % of its liquified natural gas flows, shortly after the first U.S.-Israeli strikes began. But it was not obvious what that would mean for global emissions in the near term.

Yes, countries were trying to use less of those fuels to avoid spiking costs. And, yes, plenty of nations were racing to backfill their needs with EVs or renewables. At the same time, however, several countries sought refuge in coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel of all.
It’s now evident that the bump in coal use has been offset by the stark decline in oil consumption in particular.

The question is whether this is the start of a trend — or an aberration, like the pandemic-fueled drop of 2020. The answer is hotly debated. Some analysts argue oil and gas demand will come roaring back whenever the war eventually ends. Others say it has kick-started a wave of cleantech adoption that is here to stay.

Ohio GOP circulates bill that would stymie coal plant closures
articles.description: Draft legislation obtained by Canary Media would undo a past deal to close a coal plant in 2028 — and block future settlements from shuttering similar…
paragraphs: Republican lawmakers in Ohio are circulating a plan to keep coal plants open, even if an owner has a contractual obligation to close a facility. And they hope to pass it fast, before the new Democratic governor-elect, Amy Acton, takes office.

A draft bill obtained by Canary Media would block coal-fired power plants from closing when the shutdown is required by a settlement agreement. It would apply to both past and future contracts between plant owners and private parties to resolve issues in a state court or regulatory proceeding.

“ My first thought was, ​ ‘ Why is there a piece of legislation trying to go against the Ohio Constitution?’” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest coordinator for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, referring to a prohibition against retroactive laws. ​ “ This breaks not just any contract moving forward but also breaks any previous contract.”

The proposal would directly affect the 620 -megawatt coal unit at the Cardinal power plant in eastern Ohio, which is slated to close by the end of 2028. In 2015, the Sierra Club and American Electric Power’s Ohio utility, which owned part of the plant at the time, reached a settlement in a regulatory case that included a commitment for the closure and other measures.

Under the draft bill, Buckeye Power, which took on AEP’s obligations for the Cardinal power plant following a 2022 sale, could ignore the terms of the settlement and keep the facility online if requested or ordered by various people or agencies.
In a statement sent to Canary Media, Buckeye Power said that it ​ “ supports the draft legislation and intends to file testimony in its favor after it is introduced.”

The company added that it views the proposal as ​ “ a balanced and narrowly tailored solution that helps keep electricity reliable and affordable for Ohio consumers by allowing critical generation resources to remain available until the reliability crisis has passed.”

For years, Ohio lawmakers have made it harder and harder to build renewable energy projects that would bring down electricity costs in the state while reining in greenhouse gas emissions that cause climate change.

Now, instead of reducing those barriers with a genuine all-of-the-above strategy, ​ “ they’re extending the life of these dirty, expensive coal plants,” said Democratic Rep. Tristan Rader, who is the ranking minority member on the House Energy Committee and opposes the plan. Rader said it’s unclear whether the draft bill will be considered on its own or tacked onto other legislation that is further along so it could pass in the lame-duck session. The session ends on Dec. 31. In January, Acton will move into the governor’s mansion, and Republicans will no longer have a supermajority in the House.

The draft legislation cites grid reliability as justification for the proposal, echoing the Trump administration’s assertions that aging coal plants are needed to prevent power outages. The administration has repeatedly ordered coal plants to stay open past their planned closure dates because of alleged reliability concerns. Critics say those orders are unfounded and unlawful.

articles.description: Indonesia and Norway have entered into a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) at the 31st United Nations COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.
paragraphs: Indonesia and Norway have entered into a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The agreement, facilitated by the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), marks Indonesia’s first MOPA designed to operationalise Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. It is backed by the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility.
Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.
According to the parties involved, the deal is expected to count among the largest carbon market transactions yet conducted under the Paris Agreement’s cooperative framework.

The signing ceremony took place at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31. It was witnessed by Indonesia’s Minister of Environment and Head of the Environmental Protection Agency Moh Jumhur Hidayat, and Norway’s Climate and Environment Minister Sigrun Aasland.

Following this agreement, GGGI is set to collaborate with the Indonesian government, the state electricity company PT PLN (Persero), and the Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment to establish the arrangements necessary to implement the deal.
Hidayat said: “Through this cooperation, we seek to mobilise carbon finance to support Indonesia’s energy transition and contribute to the achievement of our national climate targets.
“This cooperation will also support efforts to strengthen Indonesia’s SRUK (Carbon Unit Registry System) and ensure transparent recording and tracking of international transfers.
“Our priority is to ensure that this cooperation delivers credible mitigation outcomes, upholds environmental integrity, and is implemented in line with Indonesia’s national climate commitments.”
The MOPA will support the Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program in Indonesia, a results-based crediting mechanism built to encourage investment in additional clean, grid-connected electricity.

articles.title: Bay Area finalizes rules to boost heat-pump water heater adoption
articles.description: The first-in-the-nation air regulation will limit the sale of residential gas water heaters in the region. It goes into effect in 2028, with some major…
paragraphs: San Francisco Bay Area regulators have finalized a long-awaited rule that limits pollution from residential water heaters.

In 2023, the Bay Area Air District board passed first-in-the-nation regulations setting zero-nitrogen-oxides ( NO x) emissions standards on new home water heaters and space-heating systems sold in the region.

Last week, board members voted on final amendments for the water-heater measure, ensuring it will now take effect in 2028 — one year later than planned. The regulation includes several exemptions to address affordability concerns; about half of Bay Area installations are expected to qualify. Rules regarding the sale of home heating systems have yet to be finalized.

“ The vote is an enormous victory for clean air and the climate in the Bay Area — and really, for the nation,” said Sam Fishman, senior sustainability and resilience policy manager at the nonprofit San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association. The regulations put forward ​ “ a new model for how to transition the market away from polluting equipment in our buildings to clean equipment in a way that ensures a smooth, affordable, and equitable implementation.”
With the water-heater rules now firmly moving forward, ​ “ there’s no additional opportunity to roll them back,” Fishman noted.

The Bay Area’s newly cemented measure could guide other regulators in crafting clean-appliance rules, including those in California, Maryland, and a handful of other states that are exploring similar standards.

In the Bay Area, home to more than 7 million people, gas appliances emit more smog- and particulate-forming NO x pollution than the region’s passenger vehicles, according to the district. The bulk of those home emissions come from their fossil-fueled furnaces and water heaters.

Their pollution causes up to 85 premature deaths and 15, 000 asthma attacks in the region annually, and eliminating it would deliver health benefits valued at $ 1. 1 billion per year, according to Greg Nudd, deputy executive officer of policy at the air district. Space heating is responsible for the vast majority of the emissions.

Cost remains the main drag on heat-pump water heater adoption. On average, replacing an old gas water heater with a new gas model is about $ 3, 600, the district says, while switching to a heat-pump option is around $ 7, 100. Homeowners may also need to pay for changes to their property, like running an electrical line or remodeling a utility space, in order to accommodate the heat-pump water heater.

To address these economic barriers, regulators decided to allow certain property owners to continue to install gas water heaters: low-income households, owners of small water heaters for which heat-pump options don’t exist, and those with space or electrical constraints. Multifamily-building owners, who may need to plan system upgrades years in advance, won’t need to make the switch until 2033.
articles.lede: San Francisco Bay Area regulators have finalized a long-awaited rule that limits pollution from residential water heaters.

articles.title: The GOP lost its iron grip on Ohio. What’s the outlook for clean energy?
articles.description: A long-standing Republican trifecta has kneecapped wind and solar in Ohio. But the Democratic governor-elect and a state House shakeup could change the…
paragraphs: Democrats have finally managed to gain footing in Ohio’s halls of power — a shift that bodes well for clean energy in a state that’s become particularly hostile toward solar and wind.

Last week, voters ended Republicans’ 15 -year-long trifecta in Ohio, picking Democrat Amy Acton to be their next governor (and the first woman elected to that office). While the GOP still controls the state House and Senate, Democrats won enough seats to break Republicans’ supermajority in the House, meaning the party can no longer unilaterally override the governor’s vetoes.

From 2011 until now, Republican control of all three branches of state government has increasingly favored the oil and gas industry while limiting the growth of renewable power and scaling back energy-efficiency standards.

Acton campaigned on a different vision. Her affordability plan pledged to promote ​ “ the lowest-cost and cleanest sources of energy readily available” and to reinstate energy efficiency measures, renewable portfolio standards, and demand response programs, which incentivize customers to reduce or shift their energy consumption when the grid is strained.

In a Substack post last month, Acton wrote, ​ “ Ohio politicians have made it nearly impossible to advance zero marginal cost generation such as wind and solar,” so most of the state’s electricity comes from higher-cost fossil-fuels. ​ “ I will reexamine these obstacles that, in the long run, hit Ohio families in their pocketbooks.”

The main obstacle to utility-scale solar over the past five years has been a 2021 law, Senate Bill 52, that lets counties ban almost all such new projects within their territories. Even without an outright ban, counties can block most projects before a developer can proceed with a permit application at the state level. SB 52 also applies to wind farms of 5 megawatts or more, though almost all proposals for large-scale wind projects stopped after a 2014 budget law more than doubled the distance that turbines must be from neighboring property lines.

Over a third of Ohio counties have now designated large swaths of land as off-limits to renewables under SB 52. Acton can’t change that law and others on her own, since doing so requires legislative action.
Still, clean energy advocates are optimistic that the new governor will be able to knock down some roadblocks.
“ It’s a brand-new day here,” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest manager for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, who’s based in central Ohio.

Very soon, Acton will choose leaders for various regulatory agencies, subject to confirmation by the Ohio Senate. Those include the directors of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency and the departments that deal with health, natural resources, agriculture, and development. The Ohio EPA handles permits for fossil-fuel plants and other polluting facilities, while the Ohio Department of Natural Resources decides matters dealing with hydraulic fracturing, injection wells, and coal mining.
articles.lede: Democrats have finally managed to gain footing in Ohio’s halls of power — a shift that bodes well for clean energy in a state that’s become particularly hostile toward solar and wind.

UK by Numbers: a new website to understand the country’s biggest issues
articles.description: Explore national and local data on public spending, taxation, health, poverty, crime, and more.
paragraphs: A lot of the work I do is born out of curiosity. And frustration. Or rather, frustration at the fact that the answers to my questions are not easy to find.

If you’re familiar with Our World in Data (which is my first love and main job), it’s like that, but UK-focused. The data is more detailed (because we can dig into deeper indicators) and goes down to the subnational level.

My aim is to make the data and information behind the country’s pressing and most-discussed issues easily accessible. Everything from migration and demographics to taxation, public spending, and housing.

All of this data exists — I’m not collecting anything new here. And some government websites do good job of presenting it. But it’s often scattered around (no agency covers everything), obscure, and hard to find the latest version. I’ve tried to bring it all together in one place.

This is something I think the government should hire one or two people to do. It wouldn’t take much (in resources or money). I’m squeezing this into some free hours when I can; one or two people doing it full-time could do an even better job. It would cost the government, what, £100,000 a year?

The budget for the UK Statistics Authority is around £470 million a year. 2 This is money well-spent, and these organisations do invaluable work. But by spending just £100,000 more, they could probably multiply their impact ten-fold, if someone does it well.

Anyway, enough of my government budget-planning. You can now explore most of this data on UK by Numbers. There are still many topics to add, and things to expand on, but I thought I’d launch it now and build on it over time.

Leading small modular nuclear reactor will be late and over budget
articles.description: Ontario Power Generation is building North America’s first SMR outside Toronto. The utility says it will miss its budget goal and 2030 timeline.
paragraphs: North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.

The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades. It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond. The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX- 300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September. Developer Blue Energy has also started the NRC application process to build a BWRX- 300 in Texas.

Unlike other next-gen nuclear designs recently greenlit for construction in the U.S., GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX- 300 uses the same light-water technology that undergirds most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet today. It’s designed to produce 300 megawatts of carbon-free electricity — a substantial amount, but far less than a conventional large-scale reactor.

Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades. Just look at the latest nuclear power plants to be completed in the U.S.: Georgia Power’s Vogtle units 3 and 4, both large-scale AP- 1000 reactors that came online in 2023 and 2024, took an extra seven years and $ 17 billion to wrap up.
Nevertheless, nuclear energy is seeing resurgent financial and policy support in North America and elsewhere as demand for electricity — especially carbon-free electricity — rises.

The Darlington project is part of that wave. In total, Ontario Power Generation plans to build four units at a cost of $ 20. 9 billion Canadian, and federal and provincial investment funds have since committed up to $ 3 billion Canadian for minority stakes in the project. In the U.S., the Biden administration backed nuclear power as an anchor for an emissions-free grid, and both Trump administrations have embraced it under the banner of ​ “ energy dominance.”

Proponents of SMRs argue that smaller, repeatable designs like the BWRX will be cheaper and faster to build than large-scale reactors. The idea is that mass manufacturing and construction of these reactors will create a sort of learning-curve effect, so even if the first unit is expensive to make, the 100 th unit will be far cheaper. But right now, this is only a hypothesis. Just two SMR plants are operating commercially worldwide, in Russia and China, and some in the nuclear industry argue that it’s more economical to stick with big reactors.

Given that the Darlington project is the first attempt at building a BWRX- 300, some budget and timeline overruns aren’t surprising. Ontario Power Generation itself said that the update ​ “ reflects GE Vernova Hitachi ( GEVH) Nuclear Energy’s ongoing engineering for its first-of-a-kind SMR, which has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

“ GE Vernova Hitachi is committed to working closely with Ontario Power Generation ( OPG) and our partners to deliver the Western world’s first commercial SMR ,” a GE Vernova Hitachi spokesperson told Canary Media in an emailed statement. ​ “ While engineering and design maturity are important considerations, as OPG’s update recognizes, there are multiple interconnected contributions across engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”
articles.lede: Ontario Power Generation is building North America’s first SMR outside Toronto. The utility says it will miss its budget goal and 2030 timeline.

articles.title: The federal permitting bill has been updated. What changed?
articles.description: A(nother) conversation with Daniel Palken.
paragraphs: In Congress, the “manager’s amendment” to a piece of legislation — an updated version released by sponsors in response to feedback — is usually a matter of housekeeping, small tweaks and corrected typos. But the just-released manager’s amendment to the federal permitting bill, which everyone in DC has been eagerly awaiting, is more than that. It is intended to answer objections that have piled up since September from environmental groups, tribes, utilities, and states.

It was released on Saturday, a 494-page substitute that adds 13 new sections and changes 37 others. Protections for already-permitted projects (like offshore wind) were boosted. Transmission lost a little and gained a little. Data centers will pay even more to connect. And the bill’s authors have tried their best to address the many worries about “permit certainty.”

It arrives mere days after an election that went extremely well for Democrats, who will now dominate the next Congress. Many of them are weighing whether to take this deal or hold out for a better one next year.
What has changed and, given the election, what are its current chances of passing? Let’s get into it.
David Roberts: All right. With no further ado, Daniel Palken, welcome back to Volts. Thank you for coming.

David Roberts: There was a lot last time; now there’s a lot more. Let’s start for people who have not been tracking this as closely as the small band of obsessives on social media. Catch us up with a two-minute backgrounder on what the permitting bill is and where we are in the congressional process.

It also has targeted reforms within the Federal Power Act that will make a big difference for building out grid infrastructure, as well as reforms to geothermal, permit certainty, and hydropower, and new nuclear provisions have been added as well.

Where we stand right now is that there’s a procedural vote the day we’re recording. We should note to listeners that we’re recording at 2:00 PM on Monday, November 9th. I’m in Puerto Rico, on Atlantic time, so 1:00 PM Eastern, and we’re expecting a vote at 5:30. So we should know a lot more soon.
David Roberts: And this is a cloture vote, which is just a vote in the Senate to move forward with debating, right?
David Roberts: What are we going to learn from the cloture vote? What do Dems want to happen in the cloture vote?
articles.lede: A(nother) conversation with Daniel Palken.

articles.title: New Dem regulators plan to take on Georgia Power’s data center gas boom
articles.description: For the first time in 30 years, the state’s utility commission will have a Democratic majority — and they’re targeting Georgia Power’s costly fossil gas…
paragraphs: Georgia residents are angry at the state’s unchecked data center boom and rising electric bills — and they voted accordingly in last week’s election.
Democrats won every statewide race in Georgia, including two seats on the Public Service Commission. Republicans had held a majority at the powerful utility regulator for 30 years.

The winning candidates, Commissioner-elect Shelia Edwards and reelected Commissioner Peter Hubbard, have made clear that their top priority is to rein in rising electricity bills from Georgia Power, the state’s biggest utility. That likely means the new Democratic majority will challenge Georgia Power’s plans to enact one of the largest fossil-fuel expansions in the nation.

In December 2025, the Republican-led PSC approved Georgia Power’s plan to build nearly 10 gigawatts of new gas-fired power plants and batteries to serve proposed data centers. It did so despite recommendations from commission staff to approve only about one-third of that capacity right away, given the speculative nature of the data center growth projections that the utility used to justify its buildout.

All three Democrats on the five-member commission have signaled opposition to those plans. The two Democrats already on the commission, Hubbard and Alicia Johnson, tried earlier this year to get the PSC to reconsider the planned gas buildout but were thwarted by the GOP majority.

The five new gas-burning plants planned as part of that buildout could cost customers an estimated $ 50 billion to $ 60 billion over their multi-decade lifespan and lock in significant amounts of new greenhouse gas emissions, according to estimates from the Southern Environmental Law Center. Hubbard, who worked for 16 years in utility planning and renewable energy project development, has conducted his own analysis that found a ​ “ cost-optimized portfolio” prioritizing solar, batteries, and energy efficiency could meet expected demand and save billions of dollars compared to the utility’s gas-heavy approach.
Georgia Power’s expensive gas buildout would exacerbate the affordability challenges its customers already face.

The PSC has approved six rate hikes from Georgia Power in the past few years, increasing typical residential utility bills by 33 %, or more than $ 500 a year on average. The utility, which earns a set rate of return on what regulators allow it to spend on power plants, has seen profits swell over that same time.

“ Georgia Power is making billions while Georgia families are struggling,” Edwards, who owns a communications consulting firm, said during an Oct. 28 press event hosted by the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, a nonprofit advocacy group. ​ “ Something is fundamentally wrong with that picture.”

In February, the PSC voted 3 – 2 against a motion brought by environmental advocates to reconsider the 10 -GW gas buildout, with Hubbard and Johnson voting to block the expansion. The Democratic commissioners argued that the utility had failed to prove that data center growth justified the cost.
articles.lede: Georgia residents are angry at the state’s unchecked data center boom and rising electric bills — and they voted accordingly in last week’s election.

articles.title: The Cybertruck flopped. Electric trucks don’t have to.
articles.description: Tesla is pulling the plug on its controversial EV truck. Experts hope the next wave of electric pickups will be cheaper — and less polarizing.
paragraphs: After barely three years on the road, Tesla is planning to kick the Cybertruck to the curb after flagging sales. Elon Musk announced on Friday that the company would wind down production next year to make room for the production of Cybercabs, the robot taxis Tesla hopes will reshape transportation.

In its short lifespan, the Cybertruck managed to become a top candidate for the most polarizing vehicle on the road — ever. Critics called it a ​ “ MAGA hat on wheels” and compared it to a dumpster — a resemblance that may have fooled some hungry raccoons that once chewed on the vehicle’s rear vault. It’s already being declared ​ “ one of the greatest flops in automotive history ,” on par with Ford’s 1957 Edsel. But the polygonal, supposedly bulletproof truck did appeal to a certain demographic.

“ It’s the kind of vehicle, as a kid, you imagine for the future,” said Dan Krassner, executive director of the American EV Jobs Alliance, an advocacy organization working to end the partisan divide over electric vehicles. He’s a Republican and a wrestling fan, and noted that some of his favorite pro wrestlers drove Cybertrucks, including the married WWE superstars Seth Rollins and Becky Lynch, along with The Miz and Liv Morgan (though the latter has said it was the ​ “ worst investment” she ever made).

Weeks before the Cybertruck rolled out in late 2023, Musk told investors that Tesla would sell 250, 000 vehicles a year. But it never came close: Last year, it sold just over 20, 000. It’s the latest sign that the attempt to make EVs macho is falling flat, after Ford announced last December that its F- 150 Lightning pickup truck, the all-electric version of the country’s most popular vehicle, would be discontinued since it was a money-loser. Sales of Rivian’s electric pickup have been sliding downward each year since 2023; they have also dropped sharply for GMC’s Hummer EV, which was dubbed ​ “ the worst-selling pickup truck of 2026 .”

Automakers have long tried to shed the saintly, environmentally friendly image of the Toyota Prius, and this shift to big, aggressive electric trucks was an effort to appeal to traditional American pickup buyers. But they not only had to contend with conservatives’ hesitations about EVs; they also had to persuade a public increasingly worried about the cost of living to overcome sticker shock, to fork over thousands, if not tens of thousands, more to buy an electric pickup instead of a gas-powered one. A comparable gas-powered Ford pickup starts at $ 52, 000, about $ 11, 000 less than the Lightning did before Ford discontinued it.

“ The first electric trucks weren’t priced for the people who buy trucks, and buyers still have fair questions about charging and towing,” Krassner said. ​ “ You know, macho advertising can’t fix the monthly payment.”

The starting price for the 2026 Tesla Cybertruck was just raised to $ 92, 500, and the cheapest Hummer EV is $ 97, 200. Full-size electric pickup trucks need very large batteries to deliver the range and towing capabilities that truck buyers want, leading to higher prices, Krassner said.
articles.lede: Tesla is pulling the plug on its controversial EV truck. Experts hope the next wave of electric pickups will be cheaper — and less polarizing.
