Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
articles.description: The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
paragraphs: Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “ climate finance” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.
Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.
A civil-society tracker shows that only six nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.
Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.
Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.
As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.
Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.
This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.
articles.lede: The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

Another novel nuclear project gets green light to start construction
articles.description: X-energy received regulatory approval to break ground on a facility that will use nuclear reactors to generate power and heat for a Dow Chemical plant.
paragraphs: The United States just cleared another novel nuclear energy project to begin construction.

On Monday, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved a joint application by X-energy and Dow Chemical to build four Xe- 100 advanced nuclear reactors at a Texas industrial site owned by the Michigan-based chemicals giant. The energy plant, known as Long Mott Generating Station, does not yet have an operating license from the NRC and will not be complete until well into next decade.

The reactors will generate electricity and high-temperature steam for Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations, a facility that makes plastics and petroleum derivatives used in everything from food and beverage packaging to paints and solvents. The Seadrift facility currently relies on aging fossil-fueled equipment.

The NRC took less than 18 months to review the application, a record pace for contested hearings amid a broad-based — and controversial — effort to streamline U.S. nuclear regulation that has been in the works since the Biden administration.

“ Getting the construction permit earlier than expected is reflective of the thorough and efficient work of the NRC, the reforms that have been put in place by the Congress over the last six years, and the phenomenal work of the X-energy and Dow teams,” X-energy CEO J. Clay Sell said in a statement.

The approval comes amid a wave of federal support for new nuclear energy projects. In recent years, the U.S. Department of Energy has funded tens of billions of dollars in grants, awards, and loan guarantees to build new reactors and expand capacity at existing nuclear power plants. Support has been consistent throughout both Trump administrations as well as under the Biden administration, which viewed the carbon-free energy source as a way to decarbonize the grid. Quadrupling commercial nuclear capacity by 2050 is now official U.S. government policy.
The Xe- 100 is one of several non-water-cooled reactors, known as ​ “ Generation IV” reactors, recently granted or seeking NRC permission to begin construction.

The NRC has also greenlit construction of three molten-salt-cooled reactors by Kairos Power in Tennessee and one liquid-sodium-cooled reactor by Bill Gates–backed TerraPower in Wyoming. TerraPower and X-energy are both set to receive at least $ 2 billion each in federal funding through the DOE’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program.

The Xe- 100’s coolant of choice is helium, a lightweight, inert gas that allows the reactor to operate safely at far higher temperatures than traditional nuclear power plants. Each reactor is designed to generate up to 80 megawatts of electricity and 200 MW of thermal energy, enough to make Seadrift the first U.S. industrial site directly powered and heated by nuclear fission.

It’s the first time in nearly 60 years that the NRC has approved construction of a high-temperature gas reactor, or HTGR. The first, a 40 -MW design, produced electricity at the still-operating Peach Bottom power plant in Pennsylvania from 1966 to 1974. Another HTGR ran from 1979 to 1989 at Fort St. Vrain Generating Station in Colorado, which is now a natural-gas-fired power plant owned by Xcel Energy.
articles.lede: X-energy received regulatory approval to break ground on a facility that will use nuclear reactors to generate power and heat for a Dow Chemical plant.

Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use
articles.description: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn…
paragraphs: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project.

The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today, says that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.
This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.
As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.
However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.
(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025, 2024, 2023 and 2022 .)
Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.
The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.
articles.lede: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project.

articles.title: So, how about those midterm elections?
articles.description: A conversation with Caroline Spears of Climate Cabinet.
paragraphs: Last week’s election was a blue wave all the way down the ballot: Democrats took the House and Senate, went from 16 state trifectas to as many as 22, flipped utility commissions, and rejected data centers almost everywhere. Caroline Spears of Climate Cabinet, which won more than 100 of its 120-plus races, joins me to sort through the statehouses, PSCs, and ballot measures. Then we ask the harder questions of whether these new majorities can actually bring down costs and what it all means for climate and energy policy.
If you keep a sharp eye on the news, you may have noticed that there were some elections last Tuesday.

They were, to use the newly coined term, a bluenami. Democrats took the House by a more than 30-seat margin. Depending on how the Alaska and Mississippi races turn out, they could end up with 56 seats in the Senate, something nobody, and I mean absolutely no one, predicted. Dems are probably going to end up with 30 governorships, including in every swing state, representing more than 75% of the US population. They went from 16 state trifectas — governor, state house, and state senate — to, if Arizona goes their way, 22. And those are just the top-line changes — there’s plenty to discuss further down the ballot as well.

We’re going to discuss the scale of the bluenami, some of the lesser-know state and local races swept up in it, how it might translate to climate and energy policy, what it all portends for 2028, and much more. Let’s jump in!
Lawsuit Filed Against Money Out of Politics Proposal After Michigan Voters Pass Initiative
David Roberts: So let’s jump in. With no further ado, Caroline Spears, welcome back to Volts.

David Roberts: What a day, what a week, what a time to be alive, Caroline. Let’s start here. I think the audience knows at this point what Climate Cabinet does. You, early in election cycles, do some analysis, pick some state and lower-level races that you think matter for climate, and then get involved in those races, support those candidates, support those campaigns. So let’s just start here. How many total races were you involved in this cycle, and how many went your way?

Caroline Spears: Well, I have good news for you and bad news for you, Dave, which is that we were involved in over 120 races across more than 10 states on Tuesday. We won over 100 of them. We lost 10 of them, and we have 10 still too close to call. And the good news is that’s a win rate of over 90%.

Caroline Spears: That seems like good news. The bad news is that a year ago, I went on this pod after 2025 when we also had a great win rate, and I said, “Dave, we’re gonna go further. I promise you that we try to pick even more challenging races this year so we could keep expanding the map.”

David Roberts: Yes, ’cause too high of a win rate would suggest that you’re not taking enough chances. We discussed this last time, and you said, “All right, next time we’re gonna push, we’re gonna take even bigger chances. We’re gonna push even harder.” Apparently, you just can’t push hard enough to get ahead of the blue nami.
articles.lede: A conversation with Caroline Spears of Climate Cabinet.

articles.title: Where’s the beef? Under the solar panels.
articles.description: A Tennessee developer thinks it’s cracked the code for mixing solar panels and cattle. Scaling the model could make it easier to build clean energy in…
paragraphs: CHRISTIANA, Tenn. — As sunlight fell between the gaps in flinty November clouds, I found myself impressed by the quietness of the lawn mowers in a Middle Tennessee solar field. Instead of the obnoxious roar of diesel engines, they just produced an occasional moo.

Six months ago, Tennessee’s largest solar developer, Silicon Ranch, channeled its nomenclature and brought cattle to this 3. 25 -megawatt solar project. The 15 -member herd rotates among 15 paddocks marked out by simple electrical wire, munching Bermuda grass that grows in the shade of the panels, which sit on higher-than-usual steel piles. The cows seem amenable to the situation, judging by how plump they’ve become in that short time.

This is the first commercially viable utility-scale project combining solar and cattle farming in the U.S., according to Silicon Ranch (an earlier 2 -MW project from AES sought to prove the concept in Massachusetts’ community solar market). If the model takes off, it could boost revenues for farmers while producing more clean, cheap electricity in regions that don’t have a lot of wide-open, unused spaces to develop. And it might remedy a major obstacle to ongoing solar growth.

The U.S. builds more solar installations than any other form of power plant these days. But the industry’s upstart success story is colliding with a bulwark of local opposition from communities that don’t like the idea of this relatively new technology taking over their landscapes. One way around that conflict is to use the same land for solar power and agriculture.

The solar industry already has adopted sheep grazing as a mainstream approach to cutting grass at project sites, while supporting a secondary market for domestic meat. Researchers have also found that grasses and some crops grow better in the shade of photovoltaic panels than in an open field. But the burgeoning ​ “ agrivoltaics” sector has almost entirely excluded one of the major pillars of American agriculture — cattle ranching — for the simple reason that rambunctious bovines could easily wreck the carefully calibrated solar panels.

“ If you’re designing a solar facility that is suitable for cattle grazing, it generally requires more specific and unique design,” said Terry Jennings, principal team leader for renewable energy at the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit that studies the electricity sector. That ​ “ adds cost to the overall project, which is challenging for utilities or electric power companies.” But he noted that research on this topic is still pretty new, and a lot of uncertainty remains around ​ “ how cows really interact with the solar panels.”

To go mainstream, and help meet America’s soaring demand for electricity with more carbon-free generation, cattle-friendly solar needs to appeal to large-scale developers who rigorously maximize megawatt-hours generated per acre while minimizing cost.

In the countryside about 45 minutes southeast of its Nashville headquarters, Silicon Ranch has found that the commonly understood challenges for cattle grazing alongside solar were a little overblown.
articles.lede: As sunlight fell between the gaps in flinty November clouds, I found myself impressed by the quietness of the lawn mowers in a Middle Tennessee solar field.

Was This Really the Data Center Election?
Voters gave a big middle finger to data centers
articles.description: Democrats who campaigned on reining in data center development swept congressional and governor’s races, and voters OK’d dozens of anti–data center ballot…
paragraphs: Americans aren’t happy about the data center boom, and they made their displeasure pretty clear this Election Day. Voters not only selected a slate of Democratic candidates who campaigned against data centers; they also approved more than 30 ballot measures aimed at reining in the power-hungry facilities.

You could argue that the ​ “ data center elections” really started a year ago, when Virginians selected Democrat Abigail Spanberger as their next governor. Virginia has more than earned its status as the data center capital of the world, with the latest estimates counting more than 700 facilities around the state, and Spanberger ran on a promise to keep their intense power demand in check.

In the months that followed, it became clear that data center developers were circling in on Great Lakes states and their abundant water resources — and that fighting the facilities was a winning campaign strategy. Take Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who made data center regulation a prominent piece of his candidacy, and William Lawrence, a Democrat who won his U.S. House race after showing up at a local council meeting to fight a proposed data center.

Meanwhile in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, a three-term Democratic senator who was ousted in 2024, will return to the chamber. Brown’s campaign painted his Republican opponent as ​ “ the face of data centers,” even though it cost Brown the support of some union labor allies who’ve backed him for decades but see data centers as creators of construction jobs.

Data centers’ threat is even more palpable in Georgia and Texas, which have more projects in the pipeline than any other state except Virginia. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was easily reelected after criticizing data centers as part of his campaign and investigating their impact on power bills in the Senate. Georgia’s Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has meanwhile pledged a ​ “ pause” on new data center construction once she takes office in January. And Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored historic wins in Texas for U.S. Senate and governor, respectively, after promising to pursue a slate of data center regulations.

Anti–data center sentiment this election cycle was so strong that even some Republicans promised restrictions — Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers called for a one-year moratorium in the state, for example. But some still sided with data centers, like Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who benefited from an industry-funded ad campaign before losing a seat she had been expected to retain.
And when the data center debate showed up in ballot measures across dozens of counties and municipalities, voters gave a resounding response: Rein them in.

Data centers weren’t the only energy issue motivating voters this week. With gasoline prices at their highest level of any Election Day in U.S. history, and falling temperatures getting Americans thinking about heating bills, it’s no wonder that voters were looking for a change.
articles.lede: Americans aren’t happy about the data center boom, and they made their displeasure pretty clear this Election Day.

articles.title: U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela in July were highest since 2017
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly In July 2026, U.S. imports of crude oil from Venezuela averaged 701,000 barrels per day (b/d), the most since May 2017, before decreasing to 655,000 b/d in August, according to data published in our Petroleum Supply Monthly.

Crude oil imports from Venezuela started the year at 200,000 b/d and have steadily increased most months this year. Increased imports from Venezuela are supported by high crude oil demand from U.S. refineries because of high global refinery margins and the easing of U.S. government restrictions on purchases from the country. Many refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast ( PADD 3) are configured to process heavy sour crude oil grades, such as those from Venezuela.

According to data from Vortexa, the majority of crude oil exports from Venezuela in 2025 were destined for China. In 2026, Venezuela has exported no crude oil to China, and the United States has instead been the largest single destination by volume for Venezuelan crude oil exports.

U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela stopped shortly after the United States imposed sanctions on state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA) in January 2019. In November 2022, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control granted Chevron waivers to resume exporting crude oil from its joint venture operations in Venezuela to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries; Chevron resumed these exports in January 2023.

The U.S. government eased restrictions on PDVSA following the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and took additional measures to authorize U.S. companies to invest in the country to increase Venezuelan domestic crude oil production.

articles.title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
articles.description: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
paragraphs: That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “ state of the climate” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets. Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ ask me anything” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.
articles.lede: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.

China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
articles.description: China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
paragraphs: This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “ flat or falling” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown.
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “ wasted” wind and solar fell.

Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.

The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates. This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.

Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.
articles.lede: China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.

articles.title: Will PG&E’s $2B grid cutbacks derail California’s clean energy buildout?
articles.description: The state's utility wildfire liability conundrum could put clean energy projects in a delay doom loop — and solutions are going to be hard to come by.
paragraphs: Hello, everyone! We’ve got a lot of postelection news to cover this week. But I want to start with another hugely important issue, one that poses an existential risk to California’s utilities and a significant threat to the state’s clean energy goals — as well as a serious challenge for its incoming governor.

We’re talking, of course, about utility wildfire liability reform. Outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom failed to broker a deal with lawmakers at the end of this year’s legislative session to protect the state’s major utilities from the potentially ruinous liabilities they face from fires sparked by their power lines.

Shares of the parent companies of Pacific Gas & Electric and Southern California Edison dropped precipitously on that news. PG & E, still recovering from a 2019 bankruptcy after its equipment started the Camp Fire in 2018, responded by announcing a ​ “ strategic review” that included postponing about $ 2 billion in work planned for 2027.

Last month, PG & E sent letters to some 25, 000 customers warning them to expect delays in getting grid connections. Estimates range from one to six months for connecting housing developments and office buildings to ​ “ 2027 and beyond” for city and county transportation and public works projects.

Among those facing undetermined delays are more than 60 renewable and storage projects scheduled to be online by 2030 — which could add at least 15 gigawatts of capacity, according to a PG & E spokesperson.

This compounds the already substantial delays for clean energy developers that have been struggling to get connected to California’s transmission grid. In fact, it could undermine the financial prospects of a lot of solar projects, Jan Smutny-Jones, CEO of the Independent Energy Producers Association, said at an Oct. 28 hearing of the California Assembly Utilities and Energy Committee.

Adding to the urgency is the fact that solar developers are under the gun to complete work by 2030 or lose out on federal tax credits thanks to revised deadlines in the tax and spending megabill passed by Republicans last year. ​ “ Miss that date, game over. It’s at least a 30 % increase in the cost of those goods,” he said.

The new delays also threaten California’s goal of building 6 GW of new clean energy and storage by 2032. If projects can’t stay on schedule, the state may be forced to once again put off retiring more than 3 GW of aging, polluting coastal gas plants, Smutny-Jones said.

Mari Becker, PG & E’s vice president and treasurer, said the company has few other options if state leaders can’t protect utilities from the unbounded risk of bankruptcy in the wake of wildfires sparked by power lines. ​ “ Wildfire financial uncertainty leads to weaker credit, weaker credit leads to more expensive capital, and more expensive capital puts upward pressure on customer bills — and all of this constrains the investments that California needs,” she said.

This conundrum isn’t lost on Alex Jackson, executive director of American Clean Power–California, the state branch of the trade group American Clean Power Association. ​ “ Our preferred outcome here is that the legislature goes back to the table,” he told me.
articles.lede: The state's utility wildfire liability conundrum could put clean energy projects in a delay doom loop — and solutions are going to be hard to come by.

articles.title: Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
articles.description: The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.
paragraphs: These texts are hashed out behind closed doors in the “ blue zone” at the COP, where diplomats from nearly 200 nations – not including the US – will be haggling over each individual verb.
Over the course of the two-week summit, negotiators will be trying to reach consensus on more than 100 separate agreements – but, first, they must agree which issues are on the agenda.
The complexity of this process can make it challenging to keep track of what countries are fighting about and how negotiations are progressing.
Carbon Brief’s real-time text tracker, below, offers a helping hand by decoding the agenda and keeping a searchable record of every document for each part of the negotiations.
The first column of the interactive tracker lists the topic of each agenda item, with further columns including dates, page counts and links to the original PDFs.
The table is searchable via the interactive text box and can be sorted using the arrow icons.
This year’s talks come with a twist: Turkey holds the presidency and is hosting COP31, but Australia is jointly running the show as “ president of negotiations ”.
The pair have already announced their intention to produce a “cover text” – an overarching political document summarising key negotiated outcomes, along with issues not on the official agenda.

This could include a recognition that warming is set to “ overshoot” the 1.5C limit and the impacts this is already causing. It may also include potential solutions, such as the Turkish presidency’s “ electrification” target, for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035.
articles.lede: The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.

articles.title: Refineries have shifted production away from gasoline to middle distillates
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly Particularly high refinery margins for distillate fuel oil and jet fuel have contributed to shifts in the refinery yields of major products in 2026. Data from our latest Petroleum Supply Monthly —which includes data through August 2026—indicate refinery yields of gasoline have decreased significantly this year to support increased production of distillate fuel oil and jet fuel, sometimes referred to as middle distillates due to their relative cut points in the oil refining process.

Petroleum refinery yields represent the share of a specific fuel that is produced from each barrel of crude oil a given refinery (or group of refineries) processes. The U.S. refining fleet tends to have a strong refinery yield of gasoline—typically between 45%–50%. In general terms, for every 100 barrels of crude oil U.S. refiners process, they produce about 45–50 barrels of gasoline. Typically, the most important refinery yields in the United States are the refinery yields of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil (often sold as diesel fuel), and kerosene-type jet fuel. The combined yield of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and jet fuel typically accounts for between 85%–90% of the petroleum products produced by the U.S. refining fleet.

Despite high gasoline prices, refinery yields of motor gasoline have trended below the five-year (2021–2025) low throughout 2026. This decline largely reflects refinery efforts to shift as much of their yields as possible into the production of distillate fuel oil and jet fuel, where margins are significantly higher because of constrained global supplies for these fuels. From January through August 2026, refinery yields of gasoline have averaged less than 45% and have been well below the five-year low in every month.

Conversely, yields of distillate fuel oil have generally been higher than last year and have been above the five-year average in every month. Even more than for gasoline, crack spreads and refinery margins for distillate fuel have been elevated for most of this year in response to limits on global supplies of the fuel.

Refinery yields of jet fuel have also been relatively high this year. The U.S. refinery fleet exceeded an average jet fuel yield of 12% for the first time in March 2026, according to EIA data. Since then, the fleetwide average jet fuel yield has remained at or above 12% through the latest Petroleum Supply Monthly data for August 2026. Jet fuel yields were already setting the five-year high for most of 2025; elevated jet fuel margins in 2026 have provided a persistent incentive for refiners to continue maximizing jet fuel production.
Crude oil, gasoline, heating oil, diesel, propane, and other liquids including biofuels and natural gas liquids.
Sales, revenue and prices, power plants, fuel use, stocks, generation, trade, demand & emissions.
Forms EIA uses to collect energy data including descriptions, links to survey instructions, and additional information.

Virtual power plants can help avoid overbuilt grid if AI boom goes bust
articles.description: Paying households to reduce grid strain is a cheaper, nimbler way to meet data center demand than building electricity lines and power plants, a new…
paragraphs: Nobody really knows how much power the data center boom will need — and that’s putting utilities in a tough spot. If they underinvest in power plants and the grid, economic growth and energy reliability will suffer. But if they overinvest, Americans may pay for infrastructure nobody needs.

One way to blunt these risks, a new report says, is scaling up virtual power plants. These are networks of rooftop solar systems, home batteries, and other distributed energy equipment that utilities can control remotely to free up space on the grid we already have.

As of 2025, the U.S. had 113 gigawatts of distributed energy resources that could be used for VPPs, says the report published Thursday by consultancy The Brattle Group on behalf of The Pew Charitable Trusts. If the country can more than quadruple that capacity to 524 GW by midcentury, it could avoid the need for $ 614 billion in grid investments. In turn, the report estimates, the average household electricity bill would drop by $ 122 per year by 2050.

The findings are largely in line with previous analyses of how VPPs can save consumers money. Paying lots of homes and businesses to use less electricity or share their solar and battery power when grid demand peaks can be cheaper than building more power plants and grid infrastructure — although that relies on utility planners being confident enough that VPP capacity will dependably show up to forgo those investments.

But Brattle’s report goes a step further than past analyses, looking at how VPPs could also act as a hedge against uncertain data center demand. The report examines a hypothetical nationwide scenario in which actual load growth falls 5 % short of forecasts between now and 2030. In that scenario, overinvestment in power plants and grid infrastructure added about $ 84 billion in costs borne by U.S. utility customers from 2030 to 2040. By expanding VPPs, the report finds those overbuilding costs were reduced by $ 33 billion, or roughly 40 %.
That’s largely due to the inherent flexibility of VPPs compared to traditional utility investments, said Ryan Hledik, a principal at Brattle and lead author of the report.

“ These are smaller modular resources we can bring online, once the necessary systems are in place,” he said. ​ “ You can wait longer to figure out if that demand is actually going to appear, and then build the VPP at that point.”

These findings are valuable as utilities, regulators, and policymakers struggle to navigate a broad public backlash against data centers while still ensuring that they invest enough today to meet growing power demand.
“ I’m not envious of anyone whose job is load growth forecasting. I think they’re facing a level of uncertainty no one has faced before — certainly not in my 20 years of analysis,” Hledik said.

States are pushing utilities to impose special rules and rates to protect customers from being stuck paying for infrastructure built for data centers that never materialize, he said. However, it’s unclear how completely those policies could insulate everyday consumers, particularly in worst-case scenarios.
articles.lede: Nobody really knows how much power the data center boom will need — and that’s putting utilities in a tough spot. If they underinvest in power plants and the grid, economic growth and energy reliability will suffer.

articles.title: Top clean energy wins from the midterm elections
articles.description: Democrats look like they'll take control of state government in six more states and the utility commission in Georgia, while a few ballot measures…
paragraphs: The top story from Tuesday’s elections is clear: Democrats won big-time on the national level, dominating U.S. Senate and House races across the country. And on the state level, clean energy could get a jolt from Democratic wins for state offices and utility commissions and new approved ballot measures. Here’s a roundup of top results.

The blue wave overtook several state legislatures and governor’s mansions last night. Come January, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and likely Arizona will all have Democratic trifectas — control of both houses of the legislature and the governor’s office. And some of the states are highly likely to use that power to further climate and clean energy action.

Take Michigan, where Democrats gained control of the legislature and governor’s seat in 2022 and then used that power to enact a target of 100 % clean energy by 2040. That goal is still in place despite the Republican-controlled House’s attempt to repeal it earlier this year. Now, Democratic leaders may use their restored power to pass additional ambitious measures.

Minnesota’s Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party passed a similar clean energy mandate with the blue trifecta it won in 2022, and has the opportunity to further similar goals now that the DFL has regained control of the House.
Next door, in Wisconsin, clean energy advocates suggest the Democrats use their new trifecta to end policies that keep old, polluting power plants running and instead build more solar and batteries.

It’s only been a few years since Democrats had a trifecta in Nevada, but it’s been 60 since they controlled the Arizona legislature. Both states are among the top developers of solar power, and Arizona is rising in the ranks for battery storage. Now, they could lean even harder into clean energy.

Georgia’s Democratic sweep extended to its Public Service Commission, as voters elected two Democrats to the utility oversight board. Shelia Edwards is a new addition to the PSC, while Peter Hubbard was reelected after winning a special election last year for an abbreviated term. Democrats now have a 3 – 2 majority on the commission — a victory for the Solar Energy Industries Association, which spent to promote those candidates. The PSC is now controlled by Democrats for the first time in decades, making Georgia the only state that elects its utility commissioners with a Democratic majority.

Texas also voted blue when picking a new member of its all-Republican Railroad Commission, which oversees the state’s oil and gas industry. Democrat Jon Rosenthal beat GOP candidate Bo French, who had faced blowback for his racist comments.

Alabama’s Public Service Commission stayed in GOP hands as the two open seats went to Republicans. But the Republicans’ power will soon be diluted, as a recent law expands the three-seat commission to seven seats come January, with new members at first appointed by the governor and then gradually affirmed or replaced in elections over the next several years. Gov. Kay Ivey (R) has already named her four appointees, two of whom were nominated by Democrats.
articles.lede: The top story from Tuesday’s elections is clear: Democrats won big-time on the national level, dominating U.S. Senate and House races across the country.

articles.title: The transformative potential of solid-state transformers
articles.description: A conversation with Raghu Belur of Enphase.
paragraphs: Power electronics have taken over almost everything in our lives, with the exception, oddly, of the power grid itself — it is still held together by tens of millions of analog, iron-and-copper transformers, the design of which has barely changed in a century. Solid-state transformers replace the dumb gray box with something that can monitor and steer power or convert it from AC to DC and vice versa. In this episode, Enphase co-founder Raghu Belur, who built his company by dividing big solar inverters into thousands of small ones, explains how he’s trying the same thing with transformers, why AI data centers and big solar and battery projects are the first markets, and what it would take to put a smarter transformer on every pole.

Electricity moves long distances at high voltage, which is efficient, and gets used at low voltage, which is safe. Transformers are what step the voltage up and down along the way; every bit of power you use has passed through several. The basic design of a transformer — copper coils wrapped around an iron core — has barely changed in a century. The vast bulk of the transformers on the grid today, including the grey boxes on the top of poles you see around your neighborhood, are cheap, sturdy, and dumb as a box of rocks. Right now the US can’t make them fast enough. It takes years to get one.

Engineers have long talked about replacing conventional transformers with electronics. A solid-state transformer, mostly made of transistors, would be smaller, could handle DC as well as AC, and could actively monitor and manage the power flowing through it. The catch has always been cost — nobody needed a smart one badly enough to pay five to ten times the price of a dumb one.

That’s changing, and the two markets driving it make a somewhat awkward pair. One is solar farms and big batteries, which produce DC power. The other is AI data centers, which want more DC power inside their buildings and will pay almost anything for speed. The long-term prize, though, is not the big transformers at data centers, it’s the little ones in local communities, the gray boxes on poles where rooftop solar, EVs, and heat pumps are complicating matters.

It’s all surprisingly fascinating! My guest today, Raghu Belur, co-founded Enphase, which broke up big solar inverters into tons of smaller ones, to be tucked under each rooftop solar panel. Now he’s trying something similar with transformers, creating small modules that can be lego’d into medium or large infrastructure. Let’s get into it.
Enphase Energy Successfully Demonstrates IQ Solid-State Transformer Technology Converting 13.8 kV AC to 800 VDC
Enphase announces distributed solid-state transformer for AI data centers, targets 2028 for volume deliveries
William McMurray - Power Converter Circuits Having a High Frequency Link (US Patent 3,517,300)
David Roberts: All right then. With no further ado, Raghu Belur, welcome to Volts. Thank you so much for coming.
Raghu Belur: Good morning, David. Thank you. Thank you for having me. I’m super excited to be here.
articles.lede: A conversation with Raghu Belur of Enphase.

articles.title: A Michigan utility’s iffy plan to trap CO2 from its new gas plants
articles.description: DTE proposes building two gas plants to meet growing demand, claiming carbon capture and sequestration will help it reach state climate goals.
paragraphs: Can a utility commit to building massive gas plants and still achieve zero carbon emissions?

DTE Electric in southeast Michigan says yes, and it outlines how in a 20 -year plan currently being considered by regulators. The key, the utility says, will be carbon capture and sequestration — collecting carbon dioxide emissions from two proposed gas-fired power plants and storing them underground.

Michigan state law says power generation must be carbon-free by 2040. The gas plants would go online in 2031 and 2032, and carbon capture equipment would be added by 2035, according to the long-range integrated resource plan that DTE filed with the state public service commission in September.
The problem, as critics see it, is that carbon capture and sequestration has not been successfully deployed by electric utilities in the U.S. thus far.

Even if the technology becomes economically viable, public opposition to the technology is likely to remain strong, as evidenced by the response to the Michigan Legislature’s efforts to adopt a carbon sequestration law. Public outcry has also erupted in neighboring states over plans for carbon dioxide pipelines and injection wells.

In other words, DTE proposes to invest billions of customers’ dollars in gas plants that are dependent on a nascent and uncertain solution to comply with state law on emissions that would harm the climate and public health.
Utilities across the country are grappling with the same predicament of needing to meet steep increases in energy demand driven by data centers while also transitioning to clean energy.

DTE’s plan calls for closing the half-century-old, 3 -gigawatt Monroe coal plant and building 15 GW of renewables — mostly solar — and 4. 5 gigawatts of energy storage. The utility also proposes two new gas-fired plants totaling 2. 1 GW in the Detroit area, one of them in the same county as the coal plant. That’s more than double the amount of gas-fired generation DTE proposed to add in the long-range plan it filed four years ago. At that time, it said 946 megawatts of gas-fired generation with carbon capture could fill the gap left by the coal plant closure.

While DTE has framed the gas plants as simply replacing the retiring coal plant, clean energy advocates believe that the expanded plan is meant to accommodate upcoming data centers. DTE has signed contracts with Oracle and Google for a combined 2. 4 gigawatts’ worth of power, and its proposal cites ​ “ 2. 4 GW of new customer load” as among the changes since the 2022 plan was filed.

“ Just looking at the numbers, it’s hard not to draw that direct link,” said Helen Li, senior attorney with the nonprofit law firm Earthjustice, which represented environmentalists in regulatory proceedings over the planned Google data center.
articles.lede: DTE proposes building two gas plants to meet growing demand, claiming carbon capture and sequestration will help it reach state climate goals.

Global refinery inputs fell sharply in the second quarter of 2026 before modest recovery
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: Kpler Note: 2Q2025=second quarter of 2025 Global crude oil refinery inputs fell by 4.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), or 6%, following the start of conflict in late February in the Middle East, according to data from Kpler. Throughput then increased by 1.8 million b/d in the third quarter, primarily as refiners in the region adjusted to new trade flows.

Crude oil inputs to refineries typically increase in the second and third quarters of the year as refiners complete planned maintenance and gear up to meet peak seasonal demand for refined products, such as gasoline and jet fuel. Global crude oil inputs increased by 0.3 million b/d in the second quarter of 2025 and by another 2 million b/d in the third quarter.

The countries with the largest refining capacity in the world are the United States, China, Russia, and India. Refining in countries most directly impacted by the loss of crude oil supply from conflict in the Strait of Hormuz saw the largest declines. Crude oil refinery inputs in China fell by 2.1 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26, while crude oil inputs in India, South Korea, and Japan fell by more than 1.0 million b/d collectively in 2Q26 before rebounding by 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26.

Crude oil inputs also fell in the Middle East as the closure of the strait significantly limited the export of refined products. Crude oil inputs fell by 0.7 million b/d in Kuwait, 0.7 million b/d in the United Arab Emirates, 0.3 million b/d in Saudi Arabia, and 0.2 million b/d in Iran in 2Q26. Total crude oil inputs in these four countries increased by 0.4 million b/d in 3Q26.

Increased attacks on Russian oil infrastructure during the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine reduced refinery crude oil inputs in Russia by 0.6 million b/d in 2Q26 and an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. Russia is a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel fuel, so the decline in exports affected global diesel markets that were already tight from earlier geopolitical developments. This loss in refinery operations compounded reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September.

Although crude oil inputs were falling in some countries in the second and third quarters of 2026, they increased in the United States and in some other regions that were able to find alternative sources of supply. Crude oil refinery inputs in the United States increased by 0.5 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.5 million b/d in 3Q26, as the United States increasingly exported refined products around the world to make up for lost supply.

Global refinery crude oil inputs recovered somewhat in 3Q26, increasing by 1.8 million b/d overall as increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz, alternative routes, and ship-to-ship transfers put more Middle Eastern crude oil on the global market. Despite the increase in oil flows and refinery inputs, crude oil inputs in 3Q26 still remained about 5% lower on average than during the same period of 2025.

articles.title: Here’s how solar and wind developers can hold on to tax credits
articles.description: A Canary Forum sponsored by Intersolar & Energy Storage North America brought together industry experts to break down the shifting tax credit rules and…
paragraphs: When Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act ( IRA) in August 2022, solar and wind developers celebrated something that had historically been elusive: long-term certainty about federal tax incentives. Companies accustomed to the waxing and waning of political support for the investment tax credit ( ITC) and production tax credit ( PTC) now had a decade of reliable access to both. One analysis after the law’s passage projected an additional 155 gigawatts of solar and wind capacity by 2030 and more than $ 270 billion in additional investments.

That certainty was short-lived. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act ( OBBBA ), signed into law in July 2025, sharply shortened the timeline for wind and solar projects to claim the ITC and PTC and tightened the requirements to qualify. The OBBBA was expected to crush clean-energy growth. It didn’t. But one of its most immediate effects was to create confusion over who could still access the tax credits, for how long, and what requirements wind and solar companies must meet.

A recent Canary Media Forum, ​ “ Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline ,” aimed to cut through that confusion and offer strategies for accessing federal incentives. The event was sponsored by Intersolar & Energy Storage North America ( IESNA) and brought together a tax attorney, a project developer, a procurement specialist, and a manufacturer, who shared their perspectives on lingering uncertainties about qualifying for credits, steps to take now, and what could change in the future.

As the webinar’s title suggests, the end of 2027 is the deadline that matters most. ​ “ Those credits go away if your project isn’t placed into service by the end of 2027 ,” said Heather Cooper, a partner at the law firm McDermott Will & Schulte.

There is one exception to that 2027 cutoff. The OBBBA gave solar and wind projects one year to begin construction to retain tax credit eligibility, a countdown that ended July 4, 2026. Projects that met the July 4 deadline face a clock of their own. They generally have four calendar years after construction began to be placed in service. For projects that started this year, that means the end of 2030.

Those hard dates suggest that claiming the ITC and PTC is a black-and-white matter. It is not. Definitions for key terms such as ​ “ placed in service” and ​ “ begin construction” leave room for interpretation. For example, The Internal Revenue Service ( IRS) lists five factors it considers when determining whether a project is in service, including whether it has secured the necessary permits and licenses, completed critical preoperation tests, and synchronized with the power grid.

Because the IRS evaluates those factors case by case, Cooper said, a project doesn’t necessarily have to satisfy all five. That makes it hard to be certain when a project meets the criteria. Similarly, beginning construction doesn’t necessarily mean a project had modules installed by July 4.

Under IRS rules, one way to begin construction is to perform significant physical work, either on the project site or away from it. Another way to qualify is to pay or incur at least 5 percent of total project costs, often by purchasing modules or other equipment. And a developer that missed the July 4 deadline on paper may not be out of luck. Cooper said that reviewing what was done before that date, such as securing smaller equipment contracts, tracking internal costs, or starting early site work, may support a claim that construction had already begun.
articles.lede: When Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act ( IRA) in August 2022, solar and wind developers celebrated something that had historically been elusive: long-term certainty about federal tax incentives.

articles.title: Trump cuts have left tribes without millions of dollars for clean energy
articles.description: Canceled grants have stalled renewable energy, climate resilience, and infrastructure projects across Indian Country, adding to decades of federal…
paragraphs: Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.

The community relies on diesel for 75 % of its power, and residents put about 20 % of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the average energy burden for low-income households nationwide.

“ We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. ​ “ Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $ 20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $ 150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 % to 50 % and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.
But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $ 468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 % targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes; it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

“ The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. ​ “ And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”
articles.lede: Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year.

The International Energy Agency needs to make its data open; maybe someone can fund it
articles.description: How a mostly publicly-funded organisation still puts most of its data behind paywalls.
paragraphs: It’s hard to believe that it has been almost a decade since Hans Rosling died. He was a huge inspiration for the work I do today.
He would also be appalled that more than ten years on from his big push to make international organisations share valuable data with the world, some are still not doing it.

He coined the term “database hugging disorder” for this behaviour. One of the organisations still inflicted with the disease is the International Energy Agency (IEA). Despite being mostly publicly-funded, it makes users buy a license to access and use many of its crucial datasets.

You might have heard me beat this drum before (we’ve written about this on Our World in Data, and I’ve written about it in Nature ), but I’m here to bang it again because I still find the whole situation insane and indefensible.

I should start by saying that I think the International Energy Agency does fantastic work. It collects and produces invaluable data on energy systems across the world. I find their reports insightful. I’m glad that it exists.
It’s because their work is so valuable that locking it behind paywalls is so frustrating. If it were rubbish, I wouldn’t care.
To understand why the current situation is so mad, let me try to explain how the IEA is funded, and how it makes its money.
In 2018, the IEA’s annual core budget was around €28 million. Most of this money comes from funding from these member countries.

The remainder comes from revenue from selling its data and publications to users. It previously said that these sales were “more than one-fifth of its annual budget”. That would have been around €6 million a year.
I couldn’t find more recent public figures, but based on this data and other conversations, I still think €6 to €10 million a year is probably in the right ballpark.
articles.lede: How a mostly publicly-funded organisation still puts most of its data behind paywalls.

5 ballot proposals that could drive or derail clean energy
articles.description: A constitutional right to natural gas, a permitting revamp, and more are on the ballot in states and cities this Election Day.
paragraphs: The midterm elections are upon us. While most of the country has its eyes on who will control Congress, there’s plenty at stake for clean energy at the bottom of some voters’ ballots, too. Here are five ballot measures to keep an eye on come Tuesday night.

Proposition 45 looks to revise the California Environmental Quality Act, which for more than 50 years has governed how housing, energy, and other developers account for their environmental impacts. Specifically, this ballot measure would set a 365 -business-day time limit on most state environmental reviews, excluding fossil fuel construction. Supporters say that will allow for speedier development of clean energy and other important infrastructure. But some groups have lined up against the measure, contending that it would curb tribes’ input on projects and put California’s lands, waters, and air at risk.

Canary Media’s Alison F. Takemura has the lowdown on Eugene, Oregon’s attempt to tax major corporations to fund clean energy projects — a measure that’s similar to one already in place in Portland. Eugene residents will vote on whether to approve a fee on Amazon, Walmart, and other companies that make $ 1 billion or more in gross profits nationally and at least $ 500, 000 in gross profits within Eugene. Money raised could go toward electrifying restaurants, clean energy job training, and other climate-friendly initiatives that prioritize low-income and historically marginalized residents.

A proposed amendment to Colorado’s constitution wants to make sure households can use natural gas for cooking and heating forevermore. Amendment 82 is the brainchild of conservative advocacy group Advance Colorado, which contends that ​ “ natural gas in Colorado is under attack” as the state moves toward a zero-emissions target and as some cities look to limit gas use in new construction. Environmental and public health groups say continued reliance on the fossil fuel would saddle residents with safety risks and higher utility bills.

Voters in Michigan will consider Proposition 2, which would go further than any other state has to keep utility money out of elections. While Michigan already bars corporations, including investor-owned utilities, from donating directly to political campaigns, companies can easily sidestep those rules by funding political action committees. Proposition 2 would not only prohibit utility-funded PACs from giving to campaigns; it would also stop utility executives and their family members from donating. Utilities clearly aren’t fans of the measure: They’ve spent at least $ 215, 000 opposing it, according to the Energy and Policy Institute.

Michigan has utilities on the mind this election as residents in the city of Ann Arbor consider whether to establish a municipal utility board. If established, the board would discuss a potential takeover of investor-owned utility DTE Energy’s grid resources in the city. People opposing Proposition E say that would be an overly expensive endeavor, costing as much as $ 1 billion. Supporters think the price tag will be far smaller, and argue that a municipal utility can provide cleaner, more reliable, and more affordable power than DTE. Environmentalists and city leaders warn the proposition will derail work already underway to create a Sustainable Energy Utility in Ann Arbor; the city even sued this week to keep the proposal off the ballot.
articles.lede: A constitutional right to natural gas, a permitting revamp, and more are on the ballot in states and cities this Election Day.

articles.title: The share of solar generation with co-located battery storage is increasing
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators.

Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028.

When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment.

We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies.

Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.

articles.description: Making it easier to track data centers and power projects across the US
paragraphs: This week we launched a completely overhauled version of the Cleanview platform and many of our free tools, along with a new brand and logo.

As a company, we feel a responsibility to make our products as easy to use as possible. Companies and investors use our data to make billion dollar investment decisions. The US Senate is currently using the platform to inform policy decisions. And our free tools have been used by almost a million people over the last year.
Typically brand and product design announcements come with a lot of fluff and jargon. Today, we’ll skip that and just tell you about some new tools you might find helpful.

For each state in the US—and the country as a whole—we publish maps of every data center, renewable energy and storage project, and fossil fuel power plant. Each page also includes trends and lists of the largest projects.

On our free data center tracker page, you can see how many data centers have been built every year over the last decade. The upshot: By the end of 2026, the US will have 5 times more data centers than it did in 2016.

That same page also shows the largest data center campuses operating in the US. In our report on Amazon’s data center strategy, we wrote that the company had the largest data center operating at the beginning of this year. The company’s New Carlisle data center—built for Anthropic—surpassed 1 GW of power in March 2026.
Since then, xAI’s Colossus 2 has surged ahead. The campus now has 1.8 GW of active power. (Colossus 1 located just across the state border has another 300 MW operating).
We have similar maps, trends, and project lists for all the technologies we track, including:

To track projects, we use satellite images from a number of different sources—including some that capture images of every location on Earth every five days. Now we show many of those satellite images in the platform for our customers to see what we see. As an example, here’s what Microsoft’s Fairwater Building 2 looked like four weeks ago:

The hyperscale data center campuses we track have many buildings, each coming online at different times. Knowing when this capacity will hit the grid is important. There’s a big difference between 1 GW coming online in two years compared to ten.

articles.title: LNG imports make up increasing share of Colombia's natural gas supply
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: Gestor del Mercado de Gas Natural en Colombia (BEC), Bolsa Mercantil de Colombia (BMC) Colombia is importing more liquefied natural gas (LNG) as domestic production continues to fall. A potential drought this fall and winter could limit the availability of hydroelectric generation and boost the country’s demand for natural gas power generation. Colombia’s government has declared a national disaster in anticipation of a drought resulting from an expected strong El Niño.

Average annual marketed natural gas production in Colombia decreased from 1,070 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) in 2022 to 772 MMcf/d in 2025, according to Gestor del Mercado de Gas Natural en Columbia (BEC). Between January and August 2026, production declined further, averaging 673 MMcf/d. The fields that produce most of Colombia’s natural gas—specifically Cusiana, Cupiagua, Pauto Sur, and the offshore Guajira fields—have been declining since 2022, with no large discoveries developed to replace them. Proved reserves fell 39% to 1.7 trillion cubic feet between 2022 and 2025, according to the National Hydrocarbons Agency.

As production declined, LNG imports grew. LNG imports accounted for a record 31% of Colombia’s monthly natural gas supply in July 2026, according to data from BEC, Colombia’s gas market administrator.

Despite the increased reliance on imports, Colombia only has one operating LNG import terminal, SPEC LNG, which is located near Cartagena on the Caribbean coast. Work is under way to expand the terminal’s capacity to be online in 2026 and as early as end of October, according to Promigas. A new project, the Buenaventura LNG terminal, is targeting to startup by November 2026. In addition, the Puerto Bahia LNG Terminal and Ballenas LNG Terminal could start operations next year.

On June 11, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced that an El Niño formed in the tropical Pacific. In October 2026, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center issued an El Niño Advisory, reporting that the El Niño continues to strengthen and that there’s a greater than 83% chance of a strong to very-strong event through the first quarter of 2027. NOAA considers an El Niño event to be strong when ocean temperatures in the Niño-monitored region of the Pacific Ocean are equal to or exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius, and a very strong event occurs when ocean temperatures equal or exceed 2.0 degrees Celsius.

El Niño typically brings drier-than-normal weather to northern South America from December through February, according to NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, reducing the availability of hydropower. Natural gas consumption in Colombia’s electric power sector spiked in 2023 and 2024 when there was a strong El Niño weather pattern. In 2025, hydropower supplied 81% of the country’s electricity, natural gas supplied 8%, and coal supplied 4%. By comparison, hydropower made up 55% of the country’s electricity in March 2024, the last strong El Niño year, while natural gas-fired generation rose to 22% and coal-fired generation rose to 15%.
