The DOE announces $5B loan to Constellation for nuclear uprates
articles.description: The conditional commitment aims to boost output across 15 reactors in three states, expanding clean power capacity far faster than building new reactors.
paragraphs: On Tuesday, the U.S. Department of Energy announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $ 5 billion to boost the output of 15 reactors at eight nuclear power plants in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania by a combined 1. 1 gigawatts.

It’s the latest sign of Trump’s support for the United States’ biggest existing source of carbon-free electricity that doesn’t vary with weather conditions. It’s also the third multibillion-dollar ​ “ uprate” announcement in a month relating to Constellation Energy, which runs the plants as part of the country’s largest commercial nuclear reactor fleet.

On Sept. 30, Constellation revealed that it had finalized a power purchase agreement with Amazon in support of a 190 -megawatt uprate at its 1, 790 -MW Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Maryland. Then, on October 6, the company said it would spend $ 4. 3 billion in partnership with Google to increase generating capacity at 11 of its nuclear plants by a total of 890 MW.

Among the eight facilities announced by the DOE this week, at least six could get funding from multiple sources: the 2, 317 -MW Limerick power plant in Pennsylvania, which Constellation spokesperson Paul Adams said earlier this month would increase its output by 348 MW; the Braidwood, Byron, LaSalle, and Quad Cities plants in Illinois; and Calvert Cliffs.
A fifth DOE-backed plant in Illinois, Clinton, was already in line for a 30 -MW uprate under a 2025 deal between Constellation and Meta.
Power uprates generally involve ​ “ adding new and more efficient equipment and technology that will allow us to get more megawatts from the same plant,” Adams told Canary Media earlier this month.

The commitment from the DOE bureau formerly known as the Loan Programs Office ​ “ builds on billions of dollars in private-sector investment already supporting Constellation’s efforts to increase nuclear output,” Constellation said on Tuesday, while stressing that its announcement ​ “ does not, by itself, represent a final Constellation decision to proceed with any individual uprate or at every facility under consideration.”

It’s unclear whether the DOE’s loan commitment will benefit the same uprate projects funded by the three hyperscalers or support separate projects that will further raise the plants’ output. Constellation did not respond to a request for clarification by press time.

Still, if the uprates announced at the eight plants this week move forward, Constellation would boost its nuclear fleet’s generating capacity by about as much as a new AP 1000 reactor would — at significantly lower cost. The U.S. has thus far built only two AP 1000 s, both in Georgia, at a combined cost of more than $ 30 billion.

Nuclear energy boosters would like many more AP 1000 s to be built on U.S. soil. So would the Trump administration, which wants to see 10 new large reactors under construction by 2030 — most or all of which would probably be AP 1000 s — as part of its moon shot goal of quadrupling the country’s nuclear generating capacity by 2050.
articles.lede: The conditional commitment aims to boost output across 15 reactors in three states, expanding clean power capacity far faster than building new reactors.

articles.title: System planning and operation
The PAC taking out clean energy opponents
articles.description: A conversation with Tom Matzzie of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.
paragraphs: For years now I have been grousing to anyone who will listen that the clean electricity industry is politically feeble. It represents the cheapest, fastest-growing source of new power in the country, but it commands very little respect and inspires absolutely no fear. Last year’s Republican budget bill illustrated the point: Congress gutted the wind and solar tax credits and nobody who voted for it seemed to worry for even a moment that they would face any consequences.

It’s a truism: politicians respond less to reasoned arguments about costs and jobs than they do to threats to their own reelection. The oil industry, the NRA, and lately crypto have all figured this out, while clean energy has mostly stuck with whitepapers and persuasion.

The chair of the ITC, Tom Matzzie, is a familiar figure in my world. He came up through MoveOn and organized labor before founding the clean energy supplier CleanChoice in 2011. I want to ask him whether the ITC PAC represents a real shift in industry strategy or just one billionaire’s money, whether a PAC that targets Republicans can avoid being seen as a Democratic PAC, and what comes after November’s midterms, among other things. Let’s get into it.
Inside Climate News - Super PAC Targeting Conservatives Against Clean Energy Touts Fifth Republican Primary Win
Office of the North Carolina Governor - Governor Cooper Signs Energy Bill Including Carbon Reduction Goals Into Law
David Roberts: All right. With no further ado, Tom Matzzie, welcome to Volts. Thank you so much for coming.
David Roberts: This is juicy, Tom. We have so much to talk about, but why don’t we start here with ITC’s... Because I know at least some listeners will be wondering, the initials ITC-

David Roberts: Which is a little pun. Also, the initials of the investment tax credit, which was killed in the aforementioned bill. That’s a little Easter egg, a delightful little Easter egg. Tell me quickly the origin story of the ITC PAC. You were not a founder. It came to you-

Tom Matzzie: Yeah. I mean, I was one of the first funders of it, but really Peter Davidson and Brendan Bell at Aligned Climate Capital started phone banking some of us last fall, being like, “What are we gonna do? The super PAC effort, what’s our super PAC effort? What’s our response? We just got our butts kicked. How do we hold these people accountable?” And Peter really gets credit for, you know, calling a bunch of us and, you know, he called me because he knows my political background. You know, I ran independent expenditures in the 2006, 2008 election, pretty good years for Democrats.

And he’s like, “What do we do, Tom?” I’m like, “I’m busy, Peter.” But like, here’s what you should think about doing. You need to like find someone who’s got a soft spot who you could attack and maybe inflict some damage. Make them… You know, choose somebody who’s noisy as hell and make a big splash with it. And so to Peter’s credit, he went and talked a bunch of us into writing checks.
articles.lede: A conversation with Tom Matzzie of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.

articles.title: How much are Trump’s pro-coal policies costing us?
articles.description: A new report finds nearly half of U.S. coal plants benefit from federal handouts and pollution exemptions, harming public health, our wallets, and the…
paragraphs: The Trump administration loves coal plants. The rest of us are paying the price in higher electricity bills, poorer health, and worsening climate change.

That’s the takeaway of an analysis out today from the Environmental Defense Fund. It finds the Trump administration is directly or indirectly propping up nearly half the U.S. coal fleet with taxpayer-funded handouts, Clean Air Act exemptions, and emergency orders forcing retiring units to keep running.

These actions represent a thumb on the scale for the country’s least cost-effective and most heavily polluting source of electricity. They also serve as a promise kept: As EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin told coal and mining executives this summer, ​ “ Many of the items that were on your wish list are now done.”

“ This is a lot of government support and intervention that’s going to benefit an industry much more than it will benefit the American public,” said Surbhi Sarang, EDF’s senior attorney for clean power. “[Coal plants] produce pollution, which will just cost communities more. And they’re an expensive form of energy that will cost communities more.”
EDF’s analysis covers 184 U.S. coal plants that are operating and connected to the grid. Of those, 90 have been ​ “ propped up” in one way or another by the administration.

Seventy coal plants have received exemptions from limits on toxic pollution set by the Biden administration under the Clean Air Act. That’s allowed them to continue operating without investing in better controls. The Trump administration invited plant owners to seek these exceptions last spring, telling companies that all they had to do to skirt the regulations was send an email to a special EPA inbox.

The primary rule these plants have evaded would require them to reduce mercury pollution by 70 % and emissions of nickel, arsenic, lead, and other toxic metals by two-thirds. Those limits were projected to yield more than $ 430 million in health and other benefits for communities through 2037, according to a May press release announcing the launch of an investigation by U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) into the exemptions.
“ Coal plant pollution, including mercury and other heavy metals, can damage children’s brains and cause a lifetime of devastating illness,” Sarang said in a press release accompanying the report.

Since those exemptions were granted, the EPA has rescinded the Biden-era rule that imposed the pollution restrictions in the first place. But legal challenges could reverse that decision, Sarang said. And while the Trump administration claimed that complying with the rule would have forced plants to close down prematurely, modeling done by the Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration ​ “ showed that the costs could be absorbed and wouldn’t lead to any retirements,” she said.

EDF’s report also identifies 24 coal plants that are slated to receive a collective $ 950 million in taxpayer funds from the U.S. Department of Energy. About half of that is the $ 525 million announced in September 2025 to help refurbish up to 11 plants, according to EDF. The remaining $ 425 million, unveiled in June, is to ​ “ expand and revitalize” 13 more facilities.
articles.lede: The Trump administration loves coal plants. The rest of us are paying the price in higher electricity bills, poorer health, and worsening climate change.

articles.title: More heat pumps would actually be good for the grid, researchers find
articles.description: In states with extra grid capacity in winter, heat pumps would help lower residential electricity rates by spreading out fixed costs, according to a new…
paragraphs: Heat pumps, superefficient sources of electric heating and cooling, are winners for the climate, air quality, and typically a household’s energy bills. But a common claim cautioning against their widespread adoption in the U.S. is that the electrical grid is too strained to handle all the extra demand they would bring.

Now, a new study from clean energy think tank RMI tackles that myth. In most of the country, use of the grid maxes out in summer — during the hottest afternoons when people turn on their power-hungry air conditioners at the same time. But in winter, roughly half of states have plenty of spare capacity for heat pumps to keep homes toasty, the study found. Plus, these heat pumps wouldn’t drive up peak energy use in summer, because they would largely be displacing less efficient air conditioners.

This means that a lot of new heat pumps could be added without triggering expensive grid buildouts. But that’s not all. The study also shows that in the 24 states, plus Washington, D.C., that RMI analyzed — the places with the most spare grid capacity — heat pump adoption by some could actually help keep electricity costs more affordable for all customers.

Here’s how: Electricity rates encompass the cost of the power itself and the larger, fixed costs for the stuff that makes up the grid — the poles, wires, power plants, transformers, and other equipment — as well as regulated profits for the utility. Because it’s built to handle occasional peaks in demand, the grid is often an underutilized resource.

It’s like a toll bridge with too few cars driving on it, said Ryan Shea, study co-author and manager on the carbon-free buildings team at RMI. Because the toll is spread among far fewer customers than the bridge can handle, the cost per ride remains high. However, if more people were to use the bridge, each customer would bear less of its price tag.

Across much of the U.S., the grid is like that toll bridge. It’s built to handle the summer surge in electricity demand. But in the winter, when demand is typically less, adding consumption from heat pumps would spread out the fixed grid costs over many more kilowatt-hours.

Maximizing deployment of heat pumps over the coming years without having to build out the grid could reduce residential electricity rates by 13 % on average from what they would otherwise be due to inflation, per the study. For context, that’s equivalent to a $ 200 discount on a customer’s annual bills.

Some states have a lot more spare grid capacity in winter than others. For example, Michigan could install 3. 6 million home heat pumps and thereby lower overall residential rates by as much as 27 %. Policymakers could incentivize heat pump adoption as a tool for driving down electricity costs.
However, these numbers are directional estimates, not forecasts. The study shows where rates could fall most, Shea said. RMI didn’t have access to utility-specific data that would refine the results.

Despite that limitation, Parth Vaishnav, assistant professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan, called the work sensible and well done. He noted, though, that lower electricity rates (the price per kilowatt-hour) do not necessarily mean lower bills (the total cost for all kilowatt-hours used) for people who get heat pumps. That can especially be a concern in the coldest climes in the U.S. where electricity is substantially more expensive than fossil gas. A 2024 Michigan study Vaishnav co-authored found that switching from fossil gas to a heat pump could drive bills up for some households by more than $ 1, 000 annually under then-current fuel costs.

Building our piece of the electric stack
articles.description: A conversation with Sam D’Amico of Impulse.
paragraphs: Collectively, the electric stack (batteries, motors, chips, power electronics) has gotten about 99% cheaper since 1990. It is quietly remaking every machine that turns electricity into motion, heat, or work. Problem is, China makes most of it. Sam D’Amico, co-author of “The Electric Slide” and founder of Impulse Labs, is betting the US can still claim a piece of that stack. He’s starting with a battery-powered induction cooktop. We talk about why domestic manufacturing matters, what America would actually have to build to compete, and how Silicon Valley’s founder world really thinks about climate change, geoengineering included.

Energy analysis and journalism have traditionally focused on the supply side, but in recent years there’s been a welcome turn in the other direction, toward the ongoing revolution in the devices that consume energy. What’s happening, around the world, is an explosion of electrotech. The devices that translate electricity into motion, heat, and work are getting exponentially cheaper, smarter, and more sophisticated.

Electrotech basically comes down to four technologies: batteries, electric motors, chips, and power electronics. Together, that “electric stack” has gotten about 99 percent cheaper since 1990, which is why cars, drones, boats, and stoves keep going electric — and why, eventually, everything is going to go electric.

Currently, China manufactures most of that stack, including roughly three-quarters of the world’s lithium-ion batteries and 90 percent of the magnets that spin the motors. That leaves the US in a weak and perilous position.

One of the co-authors of that essay, Sam D’Amico, is trying to put the theory into practice. His company, Impulse Labs, makes a drool-worthy high-end induction cooktop with a battery built in. That lets it push ten kilowatts per burner while plugging into an ordinary 120V outlet. Impulse is now licensing that core platform to bigger appliance brands, and Sam has his eye on “every mid-sized machine that runs on electricity.”

I thought it would be fun to talk to Sam about why the electric stack matters, why he started with a cooktop, where electrotech might go next, and how much of it America can realistically manufacture at home. Let’s do this.

David Roberts: With no further ado, Sam D’Amico, welcome to Volts. Thank you so much for coming.

David Roberts: All right. So Sam, you were in consumer electronics in your previous life, and I’ve been sort of curious whether it was this kind of big picture thinking about electricity and the imperative of electricity and the electric stack and the evolution of global markets, et cetera, that impelled you to get into electric devices, or was it just something about cooktops specifically that lured you into this? So what prompted you to switch over?

U.S. refineries have been running at very high rates in 2026
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Petroleum Status Report The U.S. refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilization averaging more than 95% of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998. Tight global product supplies this year have boosted margins for petroleum products, particularly for diesel, incentivizing the increased run rates.
Since 1991, U.S. refinery utilization has averaged 92% from May to September, compared with 88% across the other seven months.

U.S. refineries tend to run at their highest rates between May and September to boost supply of gasoline for the peak demand season in the summer months. Distillate demand, by contrast, peaks in the fall and winter. Because refineries produce a combination of gasoline and distillates, high summer refinery utilization usually leads to an increase in distillate inventories before seasonal refinery maintenance and the peak distillate demand season.
This year the refinery runs were driven largely by tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for U.S. distillate fuel oil exports.
While refinery utilization was the highest since 1998, total U.S. refinery output was only the highest since 2019 because refining capacity has decreased by 4% since then.
In the first 3 weeks of October, U.S. refinery utilization decreased from its summer highs but remained above the five-year (2021–2025) seasonal average.

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon falls to its lowest year on record
articles.description: Rates have fallen by three-quarters in Lula’s second term.
paragraphs: This weekend, Brazil’s current president, Lula da Silva, will head to the polls against Flávio Bolsonaro (the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro). It looks like the election will be incredibly tight.
I can’t speak to all of Lula’s record, but there is one area where he has made a clear difference: in reducing deforestation in the Amazon.

The latest annual estimates of deforestation were recently published by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research (INPE). Its PRODES project uses satellite imagery to monitor the clearing of forest in the Legal Amazon. You can find this data here.
It estimates that deforestation over the past year (from August 2025 to July 2026) was around 3,300 square kilometres (km 2 ).
As you can see in the chart below, that’s a substantial fall from last year, and the lowest since records began in 1988.
Deforestation rates in the Brazilian Amazon have gone through various waves in recent decades. Lula has been quite central to some of them.
I’ve plotted the same data — annual deforestation rates — but with the bars labelled by which president was in office at the time.

Lula was president before, during the first decade of the 2000s. During his term, deforestation rates fell by three-quarters from their peak. They remained relatively stable during the next two presidents’ terms, but increased again under Jair Bolsonaro. You can see this in red.
These “peak” rates in the early 2020s were still half the rates of the early 2000s, but much higher than they had been over the previous decade.
Under Lula’s current term, they’ve fallen by roughly three-quarters again. Credit where it’s due, his government can reduce deforestation.
